utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T. The Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning, Mr. Elford.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Elford, in your testimony, and even before that, in documents that you used, that is, documents of the BritBat and other UNPROFOR units, ECMM documents and others, the terms "Vitez pocket," "the Lasva Valley," "the area of Vitez" are very frequent terms, and you used these terms in your testimony. Could you please tell us, what does this term cover, what area?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I couldn't hear the translation, so I'm looking at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness should have the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear the translation now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Should I repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think when you're talking about the Vitez pocket, the Lasva Valley, and the area of Vitez, the Vitez pocket was the area that was shown on the map, the area controlled by the HVO, whereas the Lasva Valley is more of a geographical term for the area. And I think sometimes when the term "the area of Vitez" is used, it's more the area around the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, that is not a particularly precise time. When you say "Vitez," we don't know whether you're referring to the town of Vitez or the territory of the municipality of Vitez, do we?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the term "area of Vitez" is more the area of the town, but it also can be sometimes used for areas within the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My final question about this is D52/2 has been introduced already, and this exhibit refers to the boundaries of the Vitez municipality, as a witness described them. You did see that exhibit, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen the boundaries of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could we then see on the ELMO the map with the Vitez pocket, and on which we see the boundaries of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And I will ask the witness to assist the usher with the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Elford, the boundaries, as you see them on this map, were they then copied to one of the overlays which you showed us the day before yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The overlays do not show the boundaries of the municipality, because a front line was shown on that one and which did not exactly match up with the municipality boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we're talking at cross-purposes here, but that is my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, what do you recall municipal boundaries? What do you mean by this? We are getting "frontiers" in the French translation. Do you mean administrative boundaries of the Vitez municipality, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, administrative boundaries of the municipality. As they were under the then regulations, these subdivisions were all clearly delineated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, perhaps this is my fault, perhaps I was not precise enough. Municipal boundaries, these lines that we see here in D52, you identified -- of course, you cannot know the details -- but in rough terms, those would be the boundaries of the municipality of Vitez? I've already shown you this map before. Now, are those the boundaries that you also copied to one of your overlays here?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The boundaries of the municipality are not shown on the overlays. They only show the division of the front line between the HVO and the ABiH, which is different from the municipality boundary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When looking at the Vitez Brigade documents, and you did say so the day before yesterday, we agree, I suppose, that the area of responsibility of the Vitez Brigade, in 1993, underwent certain changes. But I believe that you will also agree with me that it was always within the boundaries, within the municipal boundaries of Vitez; can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual boundaries shown on the map, on the overlays, do appear within the municipal boundaries of the Vitez pocket, but that's not to say that members of the brigade did not operate outside of the municipality area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Elford, could you please give me one example -- looking at this map, could you give us any source which could tell us that the Vitez Brigade was beyond this boundary?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't used these sources in the -- shown on the maps here. It's something that in previous documents I've seen, Viteska members being wounded or killed in the Busovaca area. But that information wasn't -- doesn't need to be shown on the map showing the area of responsibility of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a document showing that the Vitez Brigade, on the basis of any orders, as a unit, as a whole, or any of its companies, had ever been sent to the front outside the municipal boundaries, except the front at Vares?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you state for this -- I haven't seen orders that refer to areas outside the municipality boundaries, or outside of the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen an order bearing on the departure and deployment of units outside Vitez, on the front line facing the VRS, that is, the Serbs, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When compiling these maps, I didn't see orders -- I'm not sure what time period you're talking about, but not when I was compiling the front line in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Kovacic. The witness tells us that there were members of the Vitez Brigade who were deployed and killed in the area of Busovaca. That is what he said in answer to one of your previous questions. I should like to ask the witness on what is the statement based?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not evidence -- documents I've used for this report, but I believe I've seen other documents within the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I suppose that what you are talking about is a part of a different testimony and that it was an individual or individuals but not a unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it would refer to an individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that the unit, any one unit of the Vitez Brigade, that there is no document that it operated outside the municipality, outside the Vitez municipal territory, except on the front line with the Serbs, but not one of them operated ever beyond those boundaries. We do agree on that, don't we?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say I've seen documents referring to the orders to move outside of the area for the unit as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, do you know when the Vitez Brigade was formed? When you went through the documents, did you come across that information?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen information on the formation of the brigade, but it hasn't been included in this report. But the documents seem related to March of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please now distribute this batch of documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, if you're going to ask questions about the Vitez Brigade, I think I'm right in saying that the Prosecution are going to call a witness dealing specifically with the membership of that brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next witness is going to deal with the membership of the brigade. Now, it may be you're moving on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I surely will not go in the persons -- I will strictly stick to the matter of disposition and borders; no names, no individuals, exactly for the reasons just stated. I have prepared a couple -- 12 or 13 documents which might be used during the testimony, so just in order to save some time, I'm distributing that in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Elford, will you please have a look at the first document? Could the document be placed on the ELMO for the interpreters, please? Do you agree that one can conclude that Mario Cerkez was given the order by his superior, Tihomir Blaskic, and that he was appointed the commander of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. This witness has come here to produce maps about the front line, and you, Mr. Kovacic, are asking him questions about appointments and that sort of thing. Now, this doesn't arise from his evidence. You can ask questions about the maps, there is another witness to whom you can ask questions, or indeed the most sensible thing might be to produce this evidence in your own case, if you want to produce evidence as to appointments and that sort of thing. This witness really only dealt with matters of the map and force strengths. You can ask about the force strengths, the figures which he gave, or about the maps. But as far as these questions are concerned, in my view, they are not relevant to his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I entirely agree with what you said, but it was not my intention here to go on the person. It is the date when the brigade is established. The witness was talking about it and mentioned it in the report, that the brigade was established in March. I think having in mind that we have -- a conflict started in the middle of April, it is not irrelevant whether the brigade was established on the 1st March or 24th March. So it's not the person here, it's just the day of establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can you assist with this? I mean can the next witness deal with this rather than this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness will only be speaking about soldiers about whom we managed to obtain information and who seemed to have belonged to the brigade, and we do not intend to ask the next witness to tell us about the history of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Elford, to what extent can you help as to the history of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've come across information relating to the formation in the brigade in the preparation of the maps, but the maps are the main area of study for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. This is not the witness to ask about the formation of the brigade. You can ask him about the maps, you can ask him about the figures which he gave for the numbers. That's what he gave evidence about and what he has made a study of. But beyond that, you must find another witness, or indeed you can call your own evidence, which is by far the most appropriate way to deal with these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of course, I certainly will, Your Honour. But remind me just to state that the witness said the day before yesterday in his testimony that the brigade was founded in March. I'm just now trying to establish when in March; nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help, Mr. Elford, as to when in March the brigade was founded?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen this document before, and perhaps the date is consistent. I just know it was in March '93.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's as far as the witness can take it. Now let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will kindly ask the registrar to give us a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be D56/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you went through these documents or as you went through these documents, did you find any information about the Vitez Brigade, that is, about its having some barracks, some bases of its own?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information relating to the areas where headquarters of the sub-units of the brigade were based, but not information relating to actual barracks, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you come across any information to tell you that the brigade used a motel in Kruscica to train its forces for the front with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in preparation of the maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When addressing the Vitez Brigade, you said that according to some of the sources that you used, and I believe you mentioned McLeod's testimony, that when the conflict broke out, the Vitez Brigade numbered about 300 men and that it could be reinforced very rapidly through further call-ups. Could you give us some more accurate estimates as to the number of men, as to its strength in a week, in a month, in a year, how quickly? What does that mean, at least roughly?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it is difficult to give a figure for any one period of time because the brigade started with these active elements and the planning was therefore mobilization, and the mobilization would have started sometime in the April period. So we can look at figures that we have for the April period and then for the subsequent periods to show how the mobilization would have carried on, which if I was given some figures for the April period and then also figures for August and later on in '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the next document in the batch that I gave you? That is a document of the Defence Department, and this is a report on the mobilization. So the war has broken out, and the Defence office is beginning to mobilize. This is the document of the 29th of April, and I should like to draw your attention to paragraph 3 of the document, the first page, which in fact recapitulates, and that is the last paragraph at the bottom of the page in the English version, which seems to suggest that between the 15th of April and the 28th of April, that is, until the day when this report was signed, all told, about 500, that is, 498 military conscripts had been mobilized and that they had been included in units and so forth. So this document is referring to the mobilization; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first mobilization for that period, yes. I'm not sure what information it gives about -- if there was any mobilization before that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: True, one of them is basically such. Could you tell us something about the mobilization procedure because you were militarily trained and I believe you could also glean that from the documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let's move on to something else about which he did give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sir, you cannot be more precise about the term that you used, that it could mobilize very quickly, that is, within a day, a week, or a month, or something like that. We agreed about that, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the time period, but I have documents in the binder which show there was a plan for mobilization to be made, and that's the way the brigade planned to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: True. Thank you. Could we have the number for this document of the Defence Department of the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I believe you just mentioned and you also spoke about that in your testimony, Blaskic's document, the assessment of the situation. I believe it was Z4321. That is the next document in that batch. I should like to draw your attention once again to the page with an overview of the artillery. When we look at that overview, that is, the six items, can we then agree that the mortars were deployed in brigades? Page 24.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mortars in the brigades referring to the MB-120s? MBH-2?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there is also MB-120s and MBH-2s in the mixed artillery division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that is MB, because in our language, "MB" means mortar, and we understand that indication of mortars. So mortars are in the brigades, aren't they? And the brigades also have some other light artillery pieces. Then under item 6, we have a unit called "Mixed Artillery Division." That is page 24.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that unit has all the heavy artillery, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a brigade group of the artilleries that had some heavier pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think we are being precise enough. Item 6, the title is "Mixed Artillery Division." That is not a brigade. This is a document of the Operative Zone, and the commander describes the situation in the brigades; that is, items 1 to 5, and then 6, the mixed artillery unit. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What is your assessment as to the time when this document was composed?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking from the fax in the document, we're assessing for a period at least after August 1993, and probably later in the year, perhaps October of 1993. In the first paragraph, it mentions the 6th Corps of the ABiH, which we know was formed in August of 1993, and uses the terminology "ZP" on the top for "military district," which we've seen from other documents, and was from about October of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The fact remains that this document does not have a number, date, or signature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we cannot be 100 percent sure whether this is an official document or maybe if it was only a draft document of Mr. Blaskic. The informative value of this document is somewhat disputable. We cannot be 100 percent sure of it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It still provides material that can be used and correlated with other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with that. Looking at the same page, page 24, after an overview of artillery -- in the English text, it's on page 25, second paragraph on the page, at the end -- the document states that the basic problem of the artillery is the very low reserve of artillery and the impossibility of replenishment. Can we agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It refers to low reserves of ammunition and impossibility of replenishing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The document does have a number. It has been tendered into evidence; it is 432.1. Amongst other units deployed in the area of Vitez, on the basis of available information, you also mentioned the Vitezovi unit. You said that the unit was relatively weak, and bearing that in mind, the unit was not so important, according to your opinion. However, a little further down, you do mention that the unit was very well-organised, that it was very well-motivated and trained. Did you ever have an opportunity, through the documents and materials that you read, to see that that unit was active in the area, for example, of Kolonija, Rijeka, Kratine, Dubravica, Sumarija, including a centre for detention in some parts of the area of Vitez, that is, on the front line of Vitez itself; in Donja Veceriska, in the SPS factory, the explosives factory, that the unit throughout -- one police unit from its premises in 1992, and that it had some conflicts with the Territorial Defence of the BH army. Have you seen this type of information? Did you notice that this unit was mentioned on a couple of occasions in the documents that you analyzed?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I go back to the start of the question, you mentioned that I thought the unit was relatively weak. I think I was just referring to the fact that it's numerically small in size, rather than -- I think it's wrong to describe it as a weak unit, to start with, because we know it was a special forces unit. So we're not expecting it to be a large unit, but we're expecting it to perhaps have a higher morale, better training and perhaps even better equipped than the other units. As for the areas you mentioned, they weren't included in the front-line maps themselves, but I have seen documents describing the areas of activity of the Vitezovi, and it's from documents like that where we gathered the information on the size of them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You're a professional soldier, you're a military expert. You mentioned certain elements, such as level of organisation, training. These elements significantly affect the strength of a certain unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the factors that we take into account when assessing the effectiveness of a unit, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You also spoke about various reasons for -- that is, various elements, thanks to which the HVO managed to prevail in the pocket. You mentioned at one point that the HVO was capable of surviving in that area. This can be seen from certain UNPROFOR elements belonging to the British Battalion. Probably thanks to the fact that they had a lot of supplies. However, you also mentioned that the HVO was able to get supplies. This is somehow contradictory to me. Do you know how long the axis -- the supply routes were usable in the area of the Vitez pocket? Do you have any information as to that?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about a fairly large time period, which explains why the difference in the ability to supply. In the binder, the PWO reports refer to the severing of the admitted HVO supply route in approximately July 1993. It was just up until that time, there was an over-land supply route into the Vitez pocket. And then subsequent reports then talk about the aerial resupply, or the helicopter resupply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Over-land supply route, perhaps we can use the document Z1140, paragraph 2. Do you have that document in front of you?.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, excuse me. There is a slight problem with the interpretation. Here we are talking about a report about war prisoners. However, the witness is speaking about a report coming from the Prince of Wales own Regiment, because in French, we are talking about this particular document, and not the document referring to the war prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I wanted you to have a look at the document Z1140. I'm interested in paragraph 2, the last sentence of paragraph 2. According to this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has the witness got the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is in the binder that we just gave on the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would it be possible for you to tell me the footnote for the one because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you give the witness the documents we have?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody got it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So item 2, last sentence in that item. It is Z1140, I think.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a milinfosum, dated 6th of July 1993. The last sentence states as follows: "The last supply route passing via Sebesic was cut off by the BH army in the night of the 2nd of July, 1993." Could you please be so kind and show us Sebesic on the map.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: ... covered on this map because it's the area to the south of Vitez between the Route Diamond and Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] It might be too far to the south. Anyway, that's a point from the south; correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It's to the south of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that was the last supply route which the HVO could use in the pocket; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last over-land supply route, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The document has already been marked Z1140, but I do not know whether it has been admitted or not. So I would tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Admit it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me move on to another subject. You spoke at some length about the ratio of forces in the area between the BH army and the HVO throughout the year of 1993. Is it correct that we are only speaking about the year of 1993? Can we agree on that? We have limited ourselves to the year of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering the actual figures that were used yesterday, they were from 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said that the BH army was present at the moment the April conflict broke out, that it was still present at the front lines against the Serbs, and that that was the reason why the ratio of forces between the HVO and the BH army was no longer so clearly, so plainly in favour of the BH army, because part of its forces had to go to the front lines with Serbs. Could you present us with any source indicating the exact number of troops that were deployed from the BH army to the front lines against Serbs? For example, in the area of Novi Travnik, the area to the north-west of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't compiled figures for the actual numbers. I just looked at reports showing which elements of which units were deployed along the front line and some of the actions which they took part in and areas they reconquered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So as to the exact figure concerning the troops of the BH army, you cannot tell us exactly how many of its troops were deployed at the front line. We do not have any reliable information about that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the study hasn't shown the exact numbers. There is, in the BritBat reports, they do give information on units that they saw at various points, but no, I haven't carried out a further study on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You indicated that the information you compiled was compiled on the basis of certain documents concerning the presence of the HVO on the front line against the VRS, until June 1993, but you don't have any exact figures for that either. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: While describing this map, with the deployment of forces in the area of the Lasva River Valley, did you, while examining these documents, did you obtain any picture, did you form any idea as to who actually started the conflict in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't the area of my study, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, that's one of the issues we are going to have to determine. Now, Mr. Kovacic, I must insist that you restrict your cross-examination to the matters that the witness dealt with in evidence. It's not a license for a roaming cross-examination across the whole case. I'm looking at some of the documents which apparently you want to put to the witness, and I doubt very much whether they are admissible as far as he's concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour, really, but I'm just following -- I'm quitting on that issue, of course, but I'm just following the line of the Prosecution. We raised the issue yesterday before the testimony, whether we will talk about force ratio, because inevitably we are then entering other areas, or we should talk only about fronts. That is a relatively grey area, how far we may or may not, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can cross-examine the witness about what he said about the force ratio. You can question him about his knowledge, but there's little point putting to him documents which he has not seen and may know nothing about. In due course, you can comment on his evidence, of course, as you wish, but there's little point going through with him things which he knows nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, I will not. May I then just ask the witness to look at the document, the next one on my pile, which is marked in the Blaskic case with D194. My question is the following: Have you seen this document, as part of your study?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe I've seen this document and several other ABiH combat orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That document clearly deals with the ratio of forces in some of its parts. That's why it would be interesting for you. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would tender this document into evidence, but I have to draw your attention to a very serious mistake in translation. In items 3 and 4 on page 1 of the English text, a previous order of the 3rd Corps is mentioned. The number of the order is there, and it was issued on the 4th of April. Another prior order was also referred to in the previous paragraph. However, in the Croatian text, one can see that the orders in question are the orders of the 16th of April in item 3 and the order of the 15th of April in item 4. This is a significant mistake, and I would kindly ask the Prosecution to request a correction of the translation, because we will be using this document later on in the case, and I would kindly ask the document to be marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with that matter, first of all. You see the document and the point that's made. Do you accept that it says "16" in paragraph 3 in the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document mentioned by Mr. Kovacic is indeed a document that can be found in the binder presented by a witness, and the document is marked Z674 and it's a document mentioned in the footnote number 6. I think that Mr. Kovacic has a slightly different version. It is the same order which was issued by Mr. Suad Hasanovic on the 16th of April, but this document is also in our binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but the question is, is the point that he makes about the correction a right one or not? Mr. Kovacic says in paragraph 3 the order date is dated the 16th, and if one looks at the original, that appears to be right. But if you don't accept it, we'll have to have the matter examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As far as I can see in our own version, the translation actually says the 16th, so I think under that document rather than the other version, I think the proper --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The original has the same date, the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a document here. In item 3 of the original, the date is the 16th, and in item 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, it's not your fault, it is the fault of the amount of documentation that we have in this case. Now, it appears that there are two different translations. We're not going to waste any time about it now. We need to straighten this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document Mr. Kovacic has produced is a Defence exhibit from another case. I don't know who did the translation. The document that we've produced in our bundle has an official translation from the Translation Department of this Tribunal, and as far as I can see, both dates are properly recorded as the 16th of April, and it would probably be safer to proceed on the basis of our document and not bother with producing this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, while we're dealing with the documents, we received today an objection on behalf of Dario Kordic to what are described as the exhibits appended to the report. Now, I had not understood that this witness was producing documents. I thought he was merely referring to them for the purposes of his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, they would be comprehensively produced for reference by the witness. That was our understanding, and we understood that any objections -- class objections made yesterday were rejected by the Chamber in ruling the evidence to be generally -- not yesterday, the day before -- in ruling the evidence to be generally admissible. We have only had this itemized objection this morning, and we haven't had a chance to review it, but it seems to me that the probabilities are that most of the objections are of no substance, in the sense that they don't meet the permissive decision of the Chamber two days ago to allow this evidence in notwithstanding the objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, it was the report -- it was the witness's evidence that we allowed, not all these exhibits. This is a totally different matter. There was no mention made of introducing an entire bundle of exhibits. And some of the objections are of substance, because if right, they say that some of the documents are inadmissible under the Tulica ruling. What I had, and I speak entirely for myself, what I had in mind was to admit the witness's evidence about the maps and the troop strengths and not to exclude it, because it was said some of the evidence to which -- some of the material to which he had referred was ruled inadmissible. I did not have in mind ruling that all the material to which he referred then became admissible. Indeed, it isn't. So there is a totally different issue, as far as admissibility is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That may have to be resolved later. In any event, we'll have to spend some time looking at the document. In any event, the witness is able to give the evidence that he is giving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, he's able to give the evidence and he's able to say where he got the matter from, but it doesn't mean to say that that makes the evidence -- the material admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, I fully agree with what has just been said. We have admitted this witness whom you called, your office, on the basis of the fact that he was going to provide some information concerning maps because he studied them. But it has never been a question -- I mean he can rely on any information he has, but we never thought that he would be producing a number of exhibits that would be tendered into evidence, and this is not how I understood the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, typically I think experts, when they rely on material, will append the material upon which they rely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: It's not an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, even so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If he's not an expert, he's a witness collating material, and typically he will produce and append that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, and that's what I thought he was doing, and I thought out of courtesy we were provided with a copy of the documents to which he was referring so that, if necessary, we could refer to it during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There was no question of admitting those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Nice, you will be seeking to have these documents admitted --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you will be seeking to rely on these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably, yes, and probably in relation to all or nearly all. You may, I think, remember that I said right at the beginning, when I gave a general introduction to this witness, that there was a range of material that -- I may have used the words "he was going to produce," because that was my understanding, in general terms, and I said, "subject to one possible exception or qualification." And I think I had one particular qualification in mind relating to the ruling recently given by the Chamber about Blaskic's trial testimony, to which the witness has referred, as well as to the documents to be produced, and I think that was the only exception I had in mind. But we then didn't explore the matter further. But, yes, in principle, we would want the material available. Material is let in by this Chamber, understandably on a very -- I was going to say "generous basis", but generous basis, documents are let in without their being item-by-item challenged as to whether the witness is really being able to say anything about it and so on. The material then is available perhaps for later comment or for later use with other witnesses, and I have to say that my understanding was that this material would go in on the same basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Clearly, looking at the carefully drafted Defence document, much of it can go in, it appears, without objection. But there are matters where there are substantial objections; for instance, no English translation, a document missing, or, indeed, bits from Blaskic or from this trial itself. The sensible course, if I may say, is for the Prosecution to review the Defence objections and then, at some stage, to apply for admission of such documents as they want. It can be dealt as a separate issue, rather than detaining the witness while we go through it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add to clarify something, the Defence today produced some of the documents which come from this binder and tendered them as Defence documents. Don't you find it paradoxical, slightly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter whether I find it paradoxical. The fact is that they are entitled to cross-examine on documents, and, of course, that makes them exhibits. As for the other exhibits, the sensible course is for the Prosecution and Defence to agree on what can go in without objection, and then if there is anything left over, we will rule on it. Yes. And as for the document that we were discussing here, we'll make sure that we have a proper translation of it, if there's one which is mistaken. Perhaps, Mr. Kovacic, you would look into this and make sure we get the right one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I merely remind Your Honours that in the version of the translation which is in the binder, it is correct, that translation is correct. But I rely on my own documents. I do not think I'm bound to show documents that I have been given. I have my database, my sources, and this is the best document that I could find. But I found a mistake in it, and yet this document was received from the Prosecutor's office. True, not in this case. But since we are talking about documents, I assume the documents Z432.1 and Z1140 of the BritBat have not been tendered, and I should like to tender them now and ask for numbers, because we touched upon both of them and the witness confirmed that he had seen them both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number Z1140 has already been given a number, D58/2. Document 432.1 will be D59/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Let us then move on to the last subject, that is, of my concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You analysed Blaskic's orders, that is, the orders of the commander of the Operative Zone, which also covered the unit of my client. You explained the orders of the 17th of April, '93. You told us the conflict in the Vitez area or the Vitez pocket broke out on the 16th of April, '93. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, if we do agree on that, then I should like to ask you to look at the next order in this batch of documents. But, true, it is marked D269 and has a number in a circle, "145", handwritten. Yes, this document. I took this document from the Blaskic case, and this is the order of the 16th of April, 1993, at 1.30 in the morning, so that was the night between the 15th and the 16th. It is addressed to the commander of the Vitez Brigade, Mr. Cerkez, and the unit called Tvrtko, which you mentioned. Have you seen this document before, or while you made the analysis, did you see it then?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you show us on the map then, where was the Vitez Brigade to be deployed, pursuant to that order? Where was it, on the 16th of April, at sometime on that particular day; that is, after 1.30, when it was issued that order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Elford, before you answer that, have you made a close study of where the Vitez Brigade was, and I mean a close study of where the Vitez Brigade was at various times on the 16th of April, or is your evidence limited to an overall study of the force ratio?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evidence is limited to the overall study because I couldn't -- the question was where was the Vitez Brigade deployed, but this is talking about elements of the brigade. So I can say where elements were, but not where the whole brigade was at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I have made the point before, and I make it again, this is not the appropriate witness to deal with details about that day, or about these orders from Colonel Blaskic. Merely because the witness has seen them does not mean that he can assist the Trial Chamber in answering questions which are of crucial importance; namely, where precisely the brigade was at a certain time. The only people who can realistically deal with that are the people who were there. And merely looking at these orders is not going to assist us. So unless you've got any further cross-examination, we'll move on. And I mean by that, cross-examination on a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, we have been given by this witness the maps, many maps, and, for example, just one, and I'm basing it on this one, which clearly shows the development of the 17th, with the positions of the units in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which map are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What I don't know is whether the Prosecution will, at the end of the day, say, "This is the evidence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Which map are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I am referring to one of the maps we have received from the Prosecution. It is entitled "HVO Intended Front Lines in Vitez," and then it has the three positions on that day. The first one is by Blaskic's order, 4.00 in the morning of the 17th; the next one, 1815; the next one, 2210 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. You can ask about that. You can ask the witness how he got that information, where he got the information from, and on what it is based.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no dispute on that. Those orders are here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do stop arguing, Mr. Kovacic. You can put to the witness where he got the information from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You heard the question. Could you tell us on the basis of which information did you then plot the deployment of forces, as you did on this map?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The three documents that were shown on the map were exhibits in the Blaskic trial. They don't actually show the deployment or say which elements of the Viteska Brigade were deployed in these places, they show the intended defence lines, and that's what the order gave. I'm not clear what elements of the Viteska Brigade were actually sent to those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In an analysis of this nature, on the basis of individual documents, wasn't it important for you where a particular unit was the day before or the day after. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this area, I was shown the front lines that developed, I wasn't able or wasn't trying to show which elements of the brigade were at a set place at a set time. It's when you move on to the July map that it shows an overall area of responsibility for battalions, but that's the limit of it. It was really showing how the front line developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But did you say "battalions," or was that a mistake in translation? Did you say "battalions," plural?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're looking at the last map, it's showing the areas of responsibility of battalions --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me, sir. You were just talking about the 17th, and you mentioned battalions. That was my point.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said on the July map, on the 17th, I'm just showing intended lines of defence. It doesn't show which units were to be deployed there, or what size of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was later, yes, true. But do you know where the elements of all the Vitez Brigade were on the 16th of April, again, as intended -- according to the order? Which was its area of responsibility on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't made a study of where the elements were on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you did not analyze Blaskic's order of the 16th of April, that is, the one issued at half past one; you did not consider that, did you?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an order to the commander of the HVO Brigade Vitez to deploy forces, but it doesn't say which forces to deploy. And it also is covered again by the orders of the 17th, which refer to the area of Kruscica, Vranjska, and Donja Veceriska, and that those orders are included on that first map to show the development of the front lines. You can see that the lines shown in those orders match up to the lines shown on the final map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you then show us, please, on this map, on this overlay, how did that particular line which you just mentioned develop? Where did it start, during the first three days of the conflict, and where did it end?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please help the witness with the overlays.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So when the conflict broke out on the 16th of April, you show here how the forces were deployed, according to Blaskic's orders, which you mentioned, the three orders of the 17th. But you are not taking into consideration the order of the 16th, which would yet be closer to the beginning of the story. Where then, according to you, were the various elements of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Elford, let's make sure that I understand the question. You have given evidence, according to this map, based on Blaskic's orders of the 17th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are now being asked about the 16th. Can you assist us about the 16th or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question was about the units deployed at the time, and I don't have information on that. The information shown is the general intention, the general area to be covered by the front line, the defence lines, not the actual deployment of units there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, it appears this witness cannot help beyond the evidence that he's given about the 17th and the intended orders, or the intended dispositions, and it must be doubtful whether there's any point going on, trying to get evidence out of him. As I have said more than once, you can call your own evidence, you can produce these documents in your own case, but there's little point arguing with a witness who can't assist on these particular matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the orders that you had at your disposal show only the intended deployment. Not only those of the 16th, but also of the 17th. You do not really know who was where, you only know what was the intention of the commander when he issued the orders, which were the areas he wanted to get hold of. But otherwise, you don't have any other information. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It shows the intention, and that then shows how the front line subsequently developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So in that sense, there is no difference between the order of the 16th or the 17th. Both of them -- or, rather, all four of them are only about intention; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intended in the sense that the order was made. It is an order. It's not an -- it is an order to them, but implies an intention to it. It's given as an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I say one thing. If I may, I should like to remind you that at the time we received this material, we made a very serious effort to avoid precisely what we're talking about now. We're quite ready to reach an understanding about individual lines. Now, one cannot only conclude what was the intention emanating from these orders. We simply wanted to confirm where the units were, and, much to our regret, we have not managed to do that. I, nevertheless, think, in view of the documents we received, and the situation as presented by the witness, I think it is simply not realistic to speak about the 17th, which is the second day of the conflict, rather than the 16th, that is, the first order that was issued. But, as you said, there are, of course, other ways and other means of achieving that. But this is not a fair picture because it begins in the middle of the story, rather than at the beginning of it, and it is for that reason why I think that this testimony is worthless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Those are matters which you can make submissions on at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Certainly. [Interpretation] Right. Then I do not wish to waste any more of your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, going through the orders, those other orders of the 17th that you specifically mentioned, the one of 4.00, is to the units of the Frankopan Zrinjski Brigade and the Vitez Brigade; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can just refer to the actual order. The 0400 order --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] The 0400 order is addressed to Zrinjski and Viteska; right?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The next one, 1815, is addressed to Viteska, to the forward battalion of the military police, and to Zrinski; correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It then goes on to say "The commanders of the above-mentioned units are responsible to me for its execution." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are referring to item 3. So there is no subordination. All three commanders, whose units are mentioned here and then sent to individual areas, are responsible to the commander of the Operative Zone, that is, Blaskic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, because they are taking up positions along the same line, and the subordination is to the commander of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is no subordination, there is no relation of subordination among the three of them, are there?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It talks about coordination between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. Thank you. The last one of the 17th or 4th [sic], it is being issued only to the Vitez Brigade, the 2210.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you also look at other orders issued to other units in other defence sectors during that night?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just took these ones for showing the areas around Vitez for the Viteska Brigade. That's the information to show the intention in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand you. So your purpose was to show us only the positions of the Vitez Brigade or the HVO in the Lasva pocket on that particular critical day. Earlier, it seemed that you were to show all the HVO units, all the HVO forces, in the Vitez pocket, not only the Vitez municipality. Could you please explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The final map here shown shows the final front lines for the whole of the Vitez pocket. The preceding ones show some of the build-up of it from the information we had. So there was not information that I've seen for other areas of the pocket. The final map, to get the information for the whole pocket, we had to also use information from BritBat and from other sources of maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But there is no doubt then in the municipality of Vitez itself. There were different HVO units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were units other than the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And we have just seen it from these orders, haven't we, if we didn't glean it from some other documents.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders referring to, say, the Zrinski Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Quite. There is the forward battalion of the police, Tvrtko is mentioned too. So quite a number of units.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The last thing you mentioned, yes, that they're shown in areas within Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: These orders we've just been through, they are establishing the areas of responsibility of individual units at different periods of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they refer to the actual area of responsibility. These are specific orders on a specific day. I don't think it says that, for example, the Tvrtko Brigade was to always operate in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you then clarify this for me, please, Mr. Elford. If a commander decides that a particular unit is to be deployed in a particular area, in an X or Y village, and regardless of whether it's two hours, six hours, 16 days, the commander is thereby determining that unit's operational zone and the area of responsibility. I may be a layman, but that is how I understand how the army functions. Does not such an order define, by definition, also the area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of responsibility is the actual operational area. If it's sent to another area, that would be another area within the area of responsibility of another unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And when we are dealing with a number of units in one and the same area?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me for the hierarchy of units in the area, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you don't understand the question, Mr. Elford, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't feel this is an area that I've studied for this presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you showed us the front lines on the maps, conditionally speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you told us on Tuesday that you would not take more than one hour for your cross-examination. You've been at it for one hour and a half. You have to finish before the break, because we have other business. So it will be really very sensible if you finished before the break, particularly since we're dealing with the maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope I will not need more than 10 or 15 minutes. Yes, we did, indeed, dwell on these maps because the witness was saying some new things. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So as for the front lines, you do not really think they're front lines, these are the areas which should be controlled by units; that is, some units should hold individual points and individual roads. That is, I believe, how you explained it to us. Individual routes. That is, I believe, how I understood your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Areas held by units, the front line would change depending on where defensive positions were for both sides, and where attacks were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you come across any information that the HVO positions had been prepared in advance? I mean, had any engineering works been done, fortifications, trenches, or anything? But there is no such information, is there?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the preparation of this report, I'm not sure what engineering works were carried out for this specific time period. I know that there were also conflicts in the area in early 1993, January of 1993, which would have involved preparation of defence works.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Elford, my question was quite clear. Have you seen any information that the HVO had engineering positions ready, that is, trenches, cross-trenches, some fortifications, for this conflict in the Vitez pocket, for the conflict between the HVO and the army of BiH? Have you ever laid your eyes on a document that would tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information I referred to on fortifications refers to fortifications that developed at a later period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is, after the beginning of the conflict, not before the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I was reporting on the front lines that developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Elford, according to military doctrine, is there some theory about the force ratio between the offensive and the defensive forces? According to military doctrine, how much stronger need the attacker be than the defense forces, two-fold, three-fold, four-fold, or how much stronger does he need to be? If you were in the ABiH, how many men would you need to overcome the HVO in the pocket? What do the doctrines tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are a number of questions. Is there a doctrine at all that you know of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The concept of force ratio relies on many variables, and I don't think you can just talk about the numbers involved. There is evidence where small forces have defeated large forces. The numbers vary, and you have to take into account all the other factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When one thinks about it, it's a matter of common sense. I don't think we're going to get much further on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But we were told that the witness is an analyst. If he is an analyst, then he should know such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two places along the main thoroughfare through the Vitez pocket, in the area of the Vitez municipality. Both are strategically important. Would you agree that this is below Sivrino Selo, on the road, and at Grbavica, alongside the BritBat? You know what I'm talking about. Do you think these are important ABiH positions which it held there over the main road? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've shown the positions. I haven't tried to make any value judgement on the importance of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. One of your conclusions about sectors was based on a document that you used, and that was the document of the Defence Office. Did you see that the language used, the terminology, that is, there are no elevation points, there is no military idiom there, and that it is, therefore, a different document linguistically speaking than military documents issued, for instance, by Blaskic in that same area? Because it was on the basis of that document that you defined, outlined, some sectors in the Vitez valley, or rather in the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The report is written by the Defence office and explains the organisation of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You've read a number of documents, documents issued by military commanders, military units. Judging from the form of the document, do you think this is a document that was written by a military person? Let me simplify and question and let us not waste more time than necessary. This document speaks about sectors, that is, mobilization sectors, the sectors where the mobilization was supposed to be carried out. It is not a document about actual deployment. Could you agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, this document written by the Defence office relating to sectors that were established, which would be in accordance with the demand for the command of the Vitez Brigade, and the sectors they've used in this match up, then, with some of the sectors that are given in subsequent orders to sector commanders by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Only in certain parts. They do not agree completely; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's more that we only have orders for certain parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, thank you. During your analysis, did you use evidence from the Blaskic case? You did say so for certain documents, but did you also use photographs of certain positions, positions that were shown or indicated by witnesses on a model which was used in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen some of the testimony relating to the model and some of the pictures, which are not particularly good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, have you got many more minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm -- I'm just checking whether I omitted -- I mean I did omit a lot of things, but whether there's anything of crucial value. Your Honour, excuse me. I'm not sure whether you ruled or not, but I would like to enter this document from 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's nothing to do with the witness. You'll have to call him properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then if I may, just one minor thing. We had been given, the day before yesterday, after this witness concluded testimony, an additional paper also coming from the office of Defence, and I will not ask about documents. Probably that will be addressed on redirect. If it will be, I don't know. But there is again an error in translation. So if that document will be mentioned, then I will react on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you would like to speak to Mr. Lopez-Terres about it during the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would, certainly. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, just one proposal or suggestion. In the meantime, we checked the transcript from the direct examination yesterday, and on the page 14779, in line 21, the witness said the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: "... by one of the 16 of April, which was a more limited focus, just focusing on the blockade at Kruscica and Vranjska." [Interpretation] In light of that, I would kindly ask you to allow me one more question for this witness, because this is exactly what this order refers to, the order that I wanted to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Elford, the day before yesterday you mentioned, during your direct examination, that before the order of the 17th of April at 4.00, an order had been issued, the order of the 16th of April, which focused on the possibility of the attack from Kruscica and Vranjska. You have that order in your binder. Is this the order that I showed you, and were you referring to that order? I mean the order of the 16th of April issued at half past one.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the binder, if it's an order of 16th of April, half past one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Half past one in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you do have that order in your binder; right?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, the order referred to in the notes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we still do not know whether the binder will be admitted into evidence or not. But in any case, I tender this order for now as my exhibit, and I would like it to be marked as an exhibit if the binder is not being marked as yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where is the order, please, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was distributed earlier this morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can somebody assist as to which one it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I can give you mine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let's have that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the binder this order was linked to the note on page 75, and it was marked as Z672.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for this exhibit is D60/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I hope that there is no sense in wasting your time and asking the witness to show us that location on the map. Both are visible on the map, that is, south of the main route just a little bit north from Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions for the witness, in view of the questions posed to him by Mr. Sayers first and then by Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: First of all, as regards the front line where troops were deployed against the army of the Republika Srpska, Mr. Elford, in view of the documents that you have examined and analysed, do you have the impression that as of January 1993, the HVO forces progressively withdrew from the front line against Serbs so as to leave that front line only to the troops of the BH army? I'm referring to the area of Central Bosnia, of course.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there is a progressive reduction and a complete withdrawal which I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In your binder, you referred to two orders in particular; one emanating from General Blaskic, the other from General Petkovic, from January 1993. By these orders, two rotations were being requested and then a diminishment of troops deployed on the line against the Serbs; is that correct? I think the first order is dated 16th of January, and the second one, 21st of January.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen it. I'm not sure where the exact place is in the binder for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The two orders in question, do they remind you of anything as regards instructions given by HVO in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As regards the troops present in the area, Mr. Sayers asked you two days ago if, during the analysis that you undertook, you were able to establish that there had been Croatian army units, and I'm referring to the units of the army of the Republic of Croatia, in the area of Busovaca, Kiseljak, Vares and Zepce. In response to that question, you said that in the course of your work, you were not able to find any information which would suggest that there were units with the same strength of a brigade in the said area, or a battalion. This can be found on page 14840 of the 22nd of February. Is that what you said, that there were no brigades and no battalions in the area?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the areas referred to, I think my evidence of units of that size. Reportings of larger-size units were perhaps in the Gornji Vakuf and Prozor area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You have anticipated the question I was going to ask you. In the list mentioned by Mr. Sayers, the municipalities of Gornji Vakuf, Prozor and Bugojno were not mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: On the basis of several milinfosum reports, and you have seen quite a few of them for the purposes of your study, you were able to establish that in those three areas, presence or movement of troops of the army of the Republic of Croatia was mentioned on several instances; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, several instances of troop movements being seen in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I would like to show you, in connection with that, two milinfosum reports. The first one is dated 28th of May, 1993, and it is marked as Z2423.2, and another one dated 18th of June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which was marked as Z2427.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, there is an objection. Just wait. Don't hand it to the witness, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't mean to interrupt. If these milinfosums are included, obviously, within the materials that Mr. Elford relied upon, then there is no objection. But if these are new milinfosums about which no questions have been asked on cross-examination, then there is an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, can you help us? Where do these come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These two documents are not in the binder. We have prepared a binder, but the Defence has certain objections as to the admission of these documents. But it's getting increasingly more difficult for us to present certain evidence which can be commented upon by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lopez-Terres, this witness is getting out of the framework of his evidence. This witness is a member of your office, and he has come to expose certain conclusions about maps. He is not an expert, he is not an expert witness. He's not testifying to any specific area as an expert. We are basing ourselves on a certain number of maps, and we should restrict ourselves to that particular area, because we cannot pass and review all of the relevant elements through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the other day the Defence wanted to limit the area of testimony of Mr. Elford, and the Chamber decided at that time that it needed certain information as regards deployment of troops in the relevant area. This decision was taken two days ago, but contrary to what we have in the report, a question was asked regarding the number of troops of the Croatian army in the area, and this was not the subject of the report of Mr. Elford. And because that question was asked, a question concerning the presence of the soldiers of the Republic of Croatia -- and this issue is very important for the purposes of evaluation of reports on the ground -- it is very important for us to be able to ask questions to that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we do not have any additional documents. We have had enough documents. He has to base himself on the existing documents, the documents that we already have. Please ask your question, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the analysis is based on a certain number of documents, and later on the Defence may have objections as to the justification for his arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was a ruling, Mr. Lopez-Terres, not an invitation to argument. Now, would you move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
