utterances.text: Mr. Elford, in the course of your work for the Office of the Prosecutor, were you able to find -- familiarise yourself with certain documents from the HVO to the effect that certain orders were given to Croatian army units to get rid of the military insignia of the Croatian army and to put only the HVO insignia?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen documents related to the removal of HV insignia for HVO and to put on -- regarding removal of those and wearing of HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The need to remove the HV insignia, of course, had to do with the interest of being identified as HVO units?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think to avoid being identified as HV units, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In your capacity as an analyst who has worked on material concerning the HVO and the Croatian army, have you also seen documents, some of them signed by Colonel Blaskic in April of 1993, whereby units were required to compose lists of members of the Croatian army who were at the same time members of these other units?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen units like that -- orders like that which have been produced, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And then you concluded there were, indeed, HV soldiers and different units deployed in Central Bosnia and in the area of Vitez, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The order implies that there were, perhaps, people there. To be honest, it's asking for numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions regarding that subject, that is, the army of the Republic of Croatia. In your report, you also referred to a document of the 7th of May, 1993, a document issued by Colonel Blaskic, and that is an assessment of the situation. That document was annex number 3, attached to your report, and it is has the exhibit number Z891.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Have you found that document?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Would you please look at page 3, where you have the description of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Now, as regards the Muslim forces, could you read out the paragraph where we have the description of the Muslim forces, or, rather, the paragraph which refers to the structure of these forces and the materiel they have.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: [As read] "The structure: Mainly infantry units, poorly equipped. Most without military uniforms, in civilian clothes, with only battalion commanders having complete uniforms, which demonstrates that civilians are being killed. Mountain formations have a large amount of snipers in their ranks with automatic weapons and are very eager to attack the Croats."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And you can deduce from that that in May 1993, Blaskic himself described the Muslim army as an army very poorly armed, very poorly equipped.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because it's a report on the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I'm moving on to a different subject. You wrote a document, Z505, which concerns the active part of the Vitez Brigade, which had some 300 men.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Can one then conclude, after analysing this document, that the document concerning the mobilization that Mr. Kovacic spoke about some time ago, that there was a permanent standing part of the Vitez Brigade, and that that was long before the conflict broke out in April 1993, that there was a certain standing force in the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's an active element, and it included orders showing deployments of those before the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In one of the documents, and that is a report concerning the mobilization, the document issued at the end of April 1993, it mentions the mobilization of 498 persons attached to the -- and that these were the regulars of the Vitez Brigade. They constituted the active and standing part that you are referring to. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I referred to the active part of the 300, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Quite. Yes. I'm asking if in the report -- in this report, in addition to the mobilized ones, it said 498 soldiers were mobilized in addition to the regular troops of the Vitez Brigade, whether these regular troops would be those 300 men who were the active part of the brigade that you referred to. That is how you understand this.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: ... the regular part -- the active part, and then anyone else who had been mobilized before that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were asked about the boundaries of the Vitez municipality. I should like to go through some names with you, and you will tell us whether these localities fell within the area of responsibility of the accused Cerkez and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must have some regard to the clock. It must be possible to agree what was part of the boundary and what wasn't. This witness isn't a local expert, he's merely a -- not merely. He is the drawer of the map. So can we move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The order of the 16th of April, issued at half past one by Colonel Blaskic, and which was then followed by three other orders on the 17th of April, which were all mentioned, this order of the 16th of April, issued at half past one, was an order issued to Mr. Mario Cerkez and the unit Tvrtko II. We can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you tell us, or perhaps read to us paragraph 4 of that order?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 4 reads: "Personally responsible to me for the execution of the given assignments is the commander --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, because the interpreters don't have it. Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Personally responsible to me for the execution of the given assignments is the commander of the HVO Brigade Vitez, Mr. M. Cerkez."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you also tell us what was the objective of that order? Particularly, if you look at the upper left part of that order, you will find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's an administrative matter. Apparently there's a power failure in the building, and we were being asked to adjourn, but, in fact, we're going to go on until 1.00. But, Mr. Lopez-Terres, it would be helpful if we could finish this witness, please, quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Elford, this order, could you please read out who it was addressed to. You have it up there, in the upper left corner, above the hour 1.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual addressee is to the commander of the HVO Brigade. The top left corner is referring to the address of the originator. But the addressee is to the commander of the HVO Brigade Vitez, Mr. Mario Cerkez, and to the special forces unit, Tvrtko. In the top left-hand corner is the forward command post Vitez, command headquarters, Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What I'm asking -- I'm asking what is that below that?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Where it reads "combat commands"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: That is it. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads: "Combat commands in order to prevent attack activity by the enemy (extreme Muslim forces) and blockade the border territory of Kruscica, Vranjska, and Donja Veceriska."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, it is said that the forces need to take the defence area indicated, to block the village, and in case of a Muslim attack, to offset it, to neutralise it, and to prevent all movement.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Donja Veceriska, as it transpires from this order, was within the area of responsibility of the Vitez Brigade, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In this order, Mr. Cerkez is named as responsible for that operation, even though this order does not concern only his brigade but also the special unit Tvrtko. Should one, therefore, deduce from that that the brigade commander, Mario Cerkez, became also responsible for the special purpose unit which operated in his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's been given responsibility for the actions of the Tvrtko special forces unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: That is, this order gave him authority over that special forces unit, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. A responsibility over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the binder, you produced a document which is a fragment from the diary of the commander of the brigade; as such, it was developed in July 1994 by the JNA. It is in the first part, the first piece, the first item in your binder.

utterances.speaker: JON ELFORD [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you read out paragraph 115 of that manual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no need to read things out. Now, can we conclude now, please, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence asked the witness a moment ago some information about the subordination, and Mr. Sayers did the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examination and re-examination must be conducted with some regard to timing. Now, you've been re-examining, Mr. Lopez-Terres, for half an hour and more, and that, in our judgement, is enough. We can read the documents in due course and you can comment on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am reassured as you have just said that you will read the documents in due course. I have no further questions to ask to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Elford, thank you for coming to give your evidence. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, then, we will respond to the suggestion that the production of supporting material be discussed and returned to later in due course. In fact, Mr. Lopez-Terres is going to call the next witness as well, a general area of his particular interest. Just to set out a time scale of what remains for this week, because I don't know how long this power-cut is going to affect us, if at all. There's this witness. I've had no request to call the investigator who took the statement of the deceased witness, the witness I said I was going to tender, and she's available today. But absent any request to call her then, I take it, there's no challenge to the integrity of the taking of the statement. There's the language assistant, who can deal with the audiotape, and he's available today or tomorrow. I don't think he'll be very long. There are a few remaining binders to be considered, and there will be discussion then, I think, about exhibits and videos, and I have no doubt that that material can last us until lunchtime tomorrow, one way or another. But if Mr. Lopez-Terres can take the next witness, that's Carry Spork, we will use the time until the possible power-cut to the maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may make just a small suggestion. Since we may be entering the same problems of the documents with the next witness, probably it would be, for practical reasons, better to discuss the raised issue on how we will classify them, what status the documents will have, before we continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's call the witness and begin his evidence, and then we can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I say something before the witness takes the declaration? The translation into English of what I just said is not correct. It seems to have shortened -- to have cut down what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration and have a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Are you Carry Spork, 42 years old?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And you work as an investigator at the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You are Dutch by nationality?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You joined the Dutch police force in '79, and you became an investigator in 1981. And since March '96, you have been working with the Office of the Prosecutor first as an investigator seconded by the Dutch government to the Tribunal, and then, as of July '98, you have been working here within the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And you were promoted in '98 and had become the first investigator?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Spork, as an investigator at the Prosecutor's office and the team that you worked with, you conducted an investigation, and the objective of this investigation was to identify HVO soldiers who operated in the area of Vitez and who could have committed some criminal offences, these soldiers having belonged to the brigade commanded by Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And you organised an investigation. Could you please tell us something about the methodology that you used to conduct that investigation?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: First of all, we gathered 98 statements given by witnesses in relation to the happenings in the Lasva Valley. These statements were analysed by the team, and the results of that analysis were handed over to me. After we did the analyses, we formulated some kind of a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Wait a second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Apparently the power cut is starting in five minutes. We'll adjourn now until 2.00. Just one point, Mr. Lopez-Terres. I mean is this going to be another report, as it were? We haven't got a summary for this witness. We've got various documents, but if it's merely another report by an investigator, then I think you ought perhaps to look at the Tulica decision. But it may be that I've got it wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it was prepared for the Chamber, and it was handed over to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll look at that, and we better leave it at that for the power cut. We'll adjourn now until 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.25 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If Your Honour please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, will you please allow me to express the position of Mr. Cerkez' Defence regarding the actual situation, and I'll try to be as brief as possible. As you yourself have said, the Defence has not received the resume of the testimony of Mr. Spork. We have received two binders with a certain number of documents. However, we have not received any summary of his statement. So we didn't know until today what kind of approach is going to be adopted and what exactly is it that Mr. Spork will be saying. This morning Mr. Spork, on page 69, line 14, stated that he would testify using a certain methodology which consists in the following: Investigators of the OTP have analysed 98 statements of witnesses, they have made an analysis, and that analysis has been submitted to date to Mr. Spork, and he is going to testify on the basis of that document. So we are here dealing with materials that have not been admitted into evidence and the documents which represent multiple hearsay, double-hearsay evidence. So we think that the testimony of Mr. Spork -- we thought that it was going to be another report. I would like to remind this Honourable Chamber of the Tulica decision of the 29th of July, '99. In paragraph 20 on page 8, the Chamber stated that that type of evidence would be of very little if no value at all, probative value at all. So bearing in mind this ruling, the Tulica decision, we believe that the Prosecution is trying, through this witness, to circumvent the decision of the Trial Chamber that I've just quoted, so we strongly object to the testimony of Mr. Spork and we move that it be excluded from the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we join in the objection, in principle. As a matter of particular detail, I don't believe this witness gives evidence that is of concern to our client. But in principle, it appears that, as Mr. Mikulicic said, this witness is not reporting as a contemporary witness. He's collated statements and other materials for purposes of his opinions. And as Mr. Mikulicic said, on page 8, paragraph 20 of the Tulica decision, the Court said that the report therefore is of little or no probative value and will not be admitted into evidence, and it seems, as my colleague said, that that's precisely what the Prosecution seems to be wanting to do in this case. We join, in principle, with the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, when we provide a report, the Defence is objecting. When we're not supplying a document because there is no document and we are inviting a witness to testify before the Chamber in a direct manner about the nature of available information and when we call witnesses to expose results of such an analysis, Defence is again objecting. Mr. Spork is an investigator at the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal. Mr. Carry Spork has conducted an inquiry, and on the basis of that inquiry, he has made certain conclusions permitting him to identify a number of soldiers who may have been perpetrators of war crimes and who were members of the brigade of Mr. Cerkez. It is not very difficult to understand. Mr. Spork started explaining why he was tasked with that matter, together with other members of the office, and he was going to explain about the nature of documents on the basis of which he was working. And he was going to do that in an oral manner in order to facilitate the understanding of Your Honours and in order to obtain for all of us all necessary elements, all necessary information as to the documents that have been used. And as to the source of these documents, we have prepared this table which has been provided to you and on the basis of which Mr. Spork wanted to explain to you what the significance of the information is. The table, it is true, it does not speak for itself, but Mr. Spork is here to provide additional information. Here we have a document -- we have an office here, office of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lopez-Terres, you're telling us that this is the person who was in charge of this analysis, who has analysed the situation concerning the Vitez Brigade, including certain allegations of criminal behaviour. Are you telling us that -- and you have told us that you have given us this table. Is this table made on the basis of statements which are quoted on the right side of the table, so on the basis of statements that are at the disposal of your office, or is this an inquiry that was conducted on site? These are the crucial questions that the Defence is actually asking, because if this is done through statements, if they are going to speak about statements, we are within the framework of the Tulica decision, as it has been stated by the Defence. If we are dealing with certain other means of investigation, you have to tell us what exactly it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are statements, yes, and these statements represent a basis for all the work of our investigators. They are working on the basis of such statements in order to conduct their investigation. In order to identify certain individuals, if we are not able to take, for example, fingerprints, or work on-site, it is evident, it is clear, that the only elements that can be used by investigators are the elements, the information, that has been provided by witnesses and victims. They provide statements to investigators, and this is their main task. They are charged with interviewing witnesses and victims, and on the basis of such statements, they can reach certain conclusions about possible perpetrators of war crimes, including all identifying information, such as father's name, date and place of birth, and so on. So it is true that this type of information has been collected on the basis of statements given to investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it true that you were not able to call these witnesses in question to testify before the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Spork will be able to tell you more about that. All these witnesses have been selected on the basis of lists that were provided to you at the beginning of the trial. We are not talking about exterior witnesses. All these statements were given, disclosed, to the Defence at the same time as the list was provided to the Defence. So this is beyond dispute. As regards specific witnesses, there are about 50 of them who are able to provide us with some identifying information about perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I'm wondering, is it true that you were not able to call them?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could have called them to testify before the Chamber, at least part of them, but in that case, we would have 40 additional witnesses, and the only purpose of those witnesses would be to tell us the names of presumed perpetrators of war crimes. Amongst victims and witnesses, we have identified certain individuals who can provide better quality testimony. They have been selected by our office and they have testified before the Chamber, a dozen of them, and to the extent it was possible, they have confirmed the names of those presumed perpetrators. On the right side of the column, you have the actual references of the transcript, because these witnesses testified before the Chamber in this case. We have recently, on the basis of discussions that we had last year, we have compiled pages from the Blaskic transcript -- there are not that many of them, maybe two -- and that also appears on the right-hand side of the table, together with the name of the witnesses who testified either in the Kordic case or in the Blaskic case. There are other witnesses as well who are still waiting to be called. There are two witnesses among those that have been selected that we intend to call. They're living in the United States at the time, and we hope that they will be able to come. But there are certain technical difficulties, such as visas and passports, and we are not as yet sure whether we will be able to bring them here. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, let me interrupt you. What, in principle, is the difference between this witness's evidence and the evidence of the investigator in the Tulica dossier matter? Both, as far as I can see, are investigators who've examined material and, as a result, have drawn up a report; one about events in a village, the other about the brigade, the membership of the brigade, and what the brigade did. Now, just as a matter of principle, is there any distinction between the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a distinction in the sense that the investigator testifies about his investigation and his methods, and he is analysing certain material, but not in the manner as was stated in the Tulica decision. I think that this witness can add some personal value in connection with that type of evidence, and there will be certain exhibits that we would like to have admitted into evidence. They're concerning individual soldiers who were members of the said unit. These documents come from the HVO itself, and these documents can be identified here as relevant documents. Only investigators are in a position to identify those documents as such. They are the only ones who can tell us more about the HVO documents, on the basis of which we can conclude something about certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just told us -- well, we have an investigator here who is going to analyse certain witness statements. I do not know whether we are now within the framework of the Tulica decision or if we have another situation; that is, an investigator from your office who is going to analyse a certain number of documents. I forgot the name of the preceding witness. He spoke about certain maps and other documents, and he has told us about his analysis of such material. These witnesses are basing themselves on the documents that are available to your office. We cannot introduce, in a direct manner, these type of statements, because this is what you're asking. We cannot do that if we are not dealing with affidavits, but this is a different problem, a different area, concerning authenticity of documents, and so on. You cannot introduce witness statements through an investigator, we have already stated that clearly. So you can ask your witness to provide us with his analysis of documents, documents that have been obtained by your office, that could be maybe admitted by the Chamber or introduced by the Defence. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. President, we have certain documents that have been seized, emanating from the HVO. After several verifications, we believe that these documents concern soldiers of the Vitez Brigade who were implicated in the relevant events. If we present you with these documents without explaining to you how it was that we were able to identify the names of these individuals, it will be very difficult for the Chamber to understand the type of work of the Tribunal. The investigators have to base themselves on certain information, and, as I told you, these witnesses have provided names of presumed perpetrators. Our objective is not to ask you to admit, in this way, statements which we know are not going to be admitted in that way. This is only in order to explain our approach, methodological approach, to this problem. We now have, for example, 38 individuals that we believe were members of the Vitez Brigade, and we are now going to tell you, through this witness, how we were able to identify those soldiers. In view of the very high number of witnesses that have already testified before the Chamber, we thought that this might be a better way to proceed than to call witnesses just to tell us who was the individual who arrested him, and so on. We have, of course, honoured the adversarial nature of the system. All the statements have been disclosed to the Defence. What we are doing now is just to explain our methodology and tell you how these documents were obtained and what value can be attached to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid as far as that is concerned, I can see no distinction between what you want this witness to do and what you asked witnesses to do in the Tulica case. It was precisely the same thing, which was to look at witness statements and make a report upon them. Now, that is one thing to which the Defence object, and I must say, speaking for myself, I think there is force in that. On the other hand, if you want the witness to produce documents which your office has seized, that's a different matter, and he may very well be able to do that. That's a more straightforward matter, rather than the purely hearsay matter of reporting what somebody else has said. Now, that's our view. Now, if you want the witness to produce the documents, that again is a different matter. It may well be that you're entitled to do that. I see you've got one document which I've seen before, which is a list of members, for instance, of the 92nd Home Guard Brigade. If you want to produce that, then it seems to me you're probably entitled to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just contribute four very short points, listening to the discussion and debate. There are distinctions between this and the Tulica decision, because Tulica was dealing with describing a general, on-the-ground narrative, which was important to establish and which the Chamber effectively judged could be dealt with by a limited number of witnesses and not by calling the totality. In this case, as Mr. Lopez-Terres has explained, it would simply be impossible to call -- indeed we wouldn't be allowed to call by the Chamber all the witnesses simply to produce the names of perpetrators. The history of these proceedings is that where victims and witnesses have been called and have simply identified, by name, a perpetrator, someone involved, rarely, if ever, has the name itself been challenged. So to that extent it's different. We can't deal with it, we wouldn't be allowed to deal with it comprehensively, and all the indication is that there would be little, if any, challenge to the names once produced. I think it's also the case -- it may also be the case that many of the entries that Mr. Lopez-Terres would rely on relate to material that has been supported by evidence in this Chamber. Finally, without the help of this schedule in its complete form, making all due allowances for what is and what is not produced in one way or another, the Chamber will be subject to generalities about involvement of this brigade without being able to quantify, save by the most -- well, it won't be able to quantify figures of people who have been named as being involved. So bearing in mind that in your decision in Tulica you did not exclude altogether and for all purposes hearsay statements, indeed you specifically acknowledged the potential for hearsay statements to qualify as evidence in this Chamber, and given that they are only really being relied on here for picking up names which we simply wouldn't be allowed to prove by calling 60 or however many more witnesses, there are distinctions, and it's our respectful submission that this method, which I think probably parallels one of the methods known in America under the federal rules and indeed, I thought, to some degree reflected by one of the witnesses in one of the other cases in this Chamber where a summarising witness has been produced, we would urge you to say that there is a difference and that you should look at the whole of the schedule. Those are the only things I wish to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do we need, in any event, this sort of detail? Do we need to know what soldiers did what in order to determine this case? Again, I wonder about the wood and the trees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I quite understand that, if I can just speak to that point. I quite understand that point in general, but we don't know the nature of the Defence case, and indeed we won't know it until it's called. It may be going to be urged that to no extent and on no occasions were members of this brigade ever involved, and therefore -- and then it may be allowed, well, maybe one or two were involved but they would only be involved when they were engaged in a frolic of their own. And to that it would be important to know that there is evidence and material to show that there's a very large number of them named as perpetrators. Then it does become important. Now, of course, there is only a limited degree to which it's justified to forecast the Defence case, and we've been listening carefully to the cross-examination, but I don't think at the moment there's any reason to discount the possibility that it will be urged that this brigade was effectively blameless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have, first of all as a matter of principle, as I've said, ruled in general on this sort of evidence in our Tulica decision, and we don't accept that, in principle, something different is being done here. We shall accordingly rule out at this stage any evidence which is based on witness statements and the like. If it becomes a live issue as to what particular members of the brigade did, and if it is at any time suggested that the brigade was, as Mr. Kordic put it -- as Mr. Nice put it, blameless, then, of course, it may be a matter which will have to be considered in rebuttal. But at this stage, we certainly regard this evidence as falling within the Tulica decision. But we, on the other hand, will admit the evidence, insofar as it can be given, of the various exhibits which the witness produces, and so he can produce his exhibits. We'll hear any argument about that, but at the moment we would be minded to admit that and any relevant questions that you may have in relation to the exhibits, the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the witness, Mr. President, I should like to add something to what Mr. Nice said. The position of Mr. Cerkez' Defence we know says their brief in April about the things which happened in the area of responsibility of the Vitez Brigade were not committed by members of the Vitez Brigade, and ever since the accused, the brigade commander, did not know either his men, but we believed it was up to us to prove the participation of the members of his brigade and his men in these acts, and that was with only this objective in mind that we proceeded along those lines. One saw the witnesses, and reference to them can be found here in this table which was submitted to you, that every time where we wanted to produce this, then the Defence attempted to destabilise the witness, requesting a precision about the identity of soldiers and so on and so forth, or to prove that somebody was not a member of the Vitez Brigade but a member of some other brigade, or that somebody was a member of the military police but never mentioning that military police were also part of the Vitez Brigade. And they did it with all of the witnesses from Vitez who were in a position to give some names and who had come here. We compiled some documents which concerned several soldiers whose names were given to the Prosecution by the witnesses who had come here to testify, and the names were also given by some other witnesses who perhaps will come to testify here -- we hope so -- but have not done so because simply their number was very large. So this document was compiled, and it is the subject of two binders, and Mr. Carry Spork perhaps will be able to explain and clarify them to you, if you allow him to do so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, deal with those exhibits which you want the witness to produce.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Carry Spork, having identified the names of perpetrators of some crimes who could have been members of the Vitez Brigade, you also investigated if there were any documents which would concern those same witnesses; is that so?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you explain, in some detail, what kind of documents are you talking about and how did you verify this in order to ascertain that in these documents where, indeed, the -- indeed figured the names of people about whom you had information?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Most of these documents are available in our database systems. Once we had eliminated the names of people that might not be members of the Viteska Brigade because they were only mentioned once or twice or we didn't have enough particulars of them, we started screening our databases by checking the names in the database. Most of the documents we found were documents that were seized during the 1998 -- September 1998 search in the Vitez and Novi Travnik and Mostar area, and once we found these documents, we started to check -- or at least I started to check each single document and compare them with the list of names we had. As soon as we would find a document, we would try to eliminate all possibilities that the name that was mentioned was not the same one as the one that was in the document. This could be done, for instance, by checking the date of birth, because of some of the people we had the date of birth, fathers' names, places where they were born and places where they were living at that time. If you would look at the documents, some of the documents contain significant information on that, especially the date of birth, because each single soldier which was a member of the 92nd Home Guard Regiment had a specific ID number based on his date of birth plus a personal ID number, and the first -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the list, is it, of the Home Guard, Mr. Spork? I'm looking now at the document with "353" on the first front page, "353" at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: With our Exhibit number Z2332.1. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could tell us what it is first.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: This is the listing with all the members of the 92nd Home Guard Regiment, Vitez, from the period from the 8th of April 1992 until the 24th of April, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This document lists several thousand names for the period between the 8th of April, '92, until the 22nd of April, '96?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In general terms, this document, which is the document in the first binder which you put together, there are, in point of fact, 15 documents, which are all of the documents based on the lists of names; is that so?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So the list that we have just spoken about, the second document, is a list of people who died, that is, 23 who died, 63 who were wounded, in 1993, and these were by the assistant commander of the brigade, whose name was Zvonko Cilic.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Then comes a list containing some 30 -- or, rather, 35 members of a unit which was called the Alfa Force.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Then you have another list which lists the 661 wounded of the Vitez Brigade, according to the status as at the 12th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The sixth document is a list of 75 members of the Vitez Brigade, and some civilians, who were killed on the 24th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Then you have a list of members of the 3rd and 4th Battalion of the Vitez Brigade who were killed in 1993.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You also have another list of members of the Vitez Brigade who were killed or reported missing on the 20th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Then document number 9, which is again a list of killed, wounded, and missing members, between the 4th of April and the 20th of May, 1993, which was again signed by the same officer, that is, the assistant commander responsible for propaganda, Zvonimir Cilic.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The tenth document is a list of soldiers of the Vitez Brigade who were killed in the area of responsibility of the 5th Battalion, and the date of the document is the 12th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The eleventh document is, once again, a list of those members of the military police of the Vitez Brigade who were to receive some financial compensation, and that again is a document dated the 3rd of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The twelfth document is a list of soldiers of the 2nd Battalion of the Novi Travnik HVO Brigade, it was called the Novi Travnik Brigade at the time, and it is dated the 27th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The three ultimate documents are reports compiled by the investigation services of Bosnia, and they mention the names of quite a number of people they suspect of having committed crimes in the area of Vitez in June 1993, and also for the acts committed in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to draw the Chamber's attention to the fact that documents number 13 and 14 have already been admitted by your Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The documents that we are talking about are all lists of individuals. Have you found on these lists certain persons -- persons who are listed here as killed, wounded, or missing as people who were indicated by witnesses as having operated in the area of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can give the evidence. What weight we give to it is entirely for us to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I thought on another element that -- I was thinking about what you said at the beginning, that this witness would not tell us what the witnesses told him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But only the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the first volume?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the first volume, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Spork, the second volume, which covers documents 16 to 53, contains some names from the list which we have just mentioned, or not. On the other hand, it also contains specific documents which concern individuals indicated and identified.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us, what is the nature of the documents, of the specific documents, those which concern identified individuals? We spoke about lists in the first binder. Could you now, once again, briefly tell us about the documents which are compiled in the second binder.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: The documents that were compiled in the second binder mainly mention names of specific identified HVO soldiers that, according to these documents, were members of the Viteska Brigade. For instance, we have certificates of wounding and membership, we have certificates of death and membership, and we have certain certificates which show that the person was promoted to a higher rank, due to the conflict; also identifying him as being a member of the Viteska Brigade. These documents, most of the time, contain also the personal ID number of the specific person. So after comparing that with the first big list of the 92nd Home Guard Regiment, plus the other lists of documents that we spoke about before, as soon as they would have the same ID number, we could reasonably -- without reasonable doubt believe that it was about the same person. All the ones that we were not sure of, we eliminated right away, which means that if you find a document stating the certificate of wounding without saying what kind of person it actually was, or it has not been confirmed by a witness who also stated that this person was wounded, we would eliminate that name from the list of names of alleged Viteska Brigade members. If we would go into the folder, the first one, number 16, the file about Damjan Baskarad, will show us that he was first listed as a member of the 2nd Battalion, 3rd Company, which is one of the big lists. The second one is that he is listed as a member of the 92nd Home Guard Regiment, which is the list I spoke about, Your Honours, before. It continues with all the other identified HVO soldiers. Unfortunately, it is very hard to talk about this without being able to tell you how we exactly found these names, so how we started picking out these names to compare them with the documents, because they are all in relation to the witness statements. This makes it very difficult to explain how the procedure was to identify this specific person as being the one who was a member of the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: A clarification regarding the information which can be found in the table, which was submitted by the Defence and the Chamber. The figures which are in brackets, after it says "member of the 2nd Battalion, 3rd Company," could you please explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: The figure in the two brackets means that this person is listed on the original list of the 92nd Home Guard Regiment under that number. It's in chronological order, the original document, which means that if you would go to number 673 on the 92nd Home Guard Regiment list, you would find the name of Mr. Baskarad, Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: For practical reasons, we do not have to focus on only the first -- we can focus only on the first page. Mr. Spork will use the list of the regiment, the first page of the regiment.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Which?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The first page of the list of the 82nd Regiment. Only the first name which appears here under number 1, that is, the accused Mario Cerkez --

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That is correct. According to the date referred to, it should be Mr. Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And it's so that he joined the ranks of the HVO on the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That is correct. And he stayed within that area until the 26th of June -- sorry, the 6th of June, 1994, because on the 6th of June, 1994, it was renamed to the 92nd Home Guard Regiment. And so from that day on, he was a member of the 92nd Home Guard Regiment, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Number 4, do you find again that name amongst the documents on the basis of which you could individualise him, that is, the name of Karlo Grabovac.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The same goes for number 7, Ivica Drmic.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Once again, and I will finish shortly, all the numbers that appear under the title "Members of the 92nd Home Guard Brigade" are numbers who can be found on the longer list consisting of several thousand names, and where we can find the name of the soldier concerned.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were able to find -- to identify documents concerning 38 soldiers exactly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: If I understand correctly what you say, you also dispose of a much larger number of documents, and you are sure that these documents -- these documents here concern the 38 soldiers in question.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: If there was any doubt as to the identity or the link between the document and the identity, you did not take that into account; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, sir. We eliminated that document right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Amongst the soldiers that you have identified, and you have quoted names of several soldiers, for example, having the same name Baskarad, you were also able to find an individual by the name of Krunoslav Bonic amongst these individuals.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The name of this soldier can be found on the Vitez Brigade list, and this soldier was listed as missing in that particular document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The same goes for the individual by the name of Miroslav Bobas.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As regard the individual named Miroslav Bralo, you have also found documents testifying to the fact that he was a member of the Vitez Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Zvonimir Cilic, we have already mentioned him, because he was the one who compiled the first list, he too was a member of the Vitez Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Borislav Jozic was also a member of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And he died during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: According to the documents we have, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were also able to find information and documents on the basis of which you were able to conclude that Anto Kovac was a member of the police unit of the Vitez Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. We found documents which listed him as a wounded member of the Vitez Brigade military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The same goes for Nevenko or Nevenko Kovac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He was listed as being killed in the zone of responsibility of the 5th Battalion, and we found another document which confirmed that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Zlatko Nakic was also a member of the military police of the said brigade?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He's listed in the document as a killed member of the brigade military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Nenad Santic, you have several documents about him, permitting you to conclude that he too was a member of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And the same goes for all other soldiers whose names appear on this list?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: There is something particular as regards an individual named Perica Vukadinovic. Could you please tell us, in a few words, to what facts the individual by the name of Vukadinovic can be associated?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: To what specific events that took place in Vitez can the name of Perica Vukadinovic be linked? I have in mind the events that took place in May 1992, the murder of Semir Trako.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard evidence about this from some other witnesses, that this individual was suspected of that offence, so there's no need to go over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But perhaps we could deal with one, since we are dealing with that one. The last named soldier is called Kriss Wilson?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The file concerning this individual was the last file that was compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Spork, what can you tell us about this particular file, file number 53 of the binder?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a British mercenary named Kriss Wilson who joined the HVO as a mercenary. He has never been identified by any of the witnesses. But while we did the search, we found documents indicating that he was the commander of the so-called Alfa Force, and because of that we also found that he was on the list of salaries of the Vitez Alfa Force sabotage group for the month -- on the month of June 1992, which indicates that he must have been a member before that. Otherwise, he couldn't have been on the salary list. Then we have a certificate of wounding, which is specifically naming this person, and it says that he was wounded on the 14th of October, 1992, in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I think we had some evidence of that. I seem to remember that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Kriss Wilson was wounded on the 14th of October, 1992, in combat in Novi Travnik, as you have just said. He was examined by doctors, and a report was compiled thereof. This report can be found in the file under Z2663.2. Do you have this report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but it's Z2663.3 is the English translation, and it's number --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. As far as this English translation is concerned, could you show me, on the translation, the column which speaks about his immediate superior? What is the name that appears in that part of the report?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: It says that his direct superior was Mr. Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This took place during a conflict with the BH army. This individual was wounded during that conflict on the 14th of October, 1992, in Novi Travnik, according to the medical report that we have. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct. The certificate also says: "During combat and immediate preparations for combat, the above-named was wounded by fragmentation ammunition fired by an enemy sniper."

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: There is something special about Zoran Sero, and this is the last name I will be referring to. His file is listed under number 48 in the binder. Excuse me, I misspoke. Forty-seven.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: According to the information we have, he was listed as a member of the Alfa Force and also listed as being killed. The evidence, number Z1372.1 says that Zoran Nikica Sero, born in 1962, was killed on the 18th of June, 1993, in Stari Vitez, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You have a document here, a military identity card that is reproduced here as Exhibit Z142, dated 26th of June, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This document indicates, on the back page, under the name of Zoran Sero, the 1st Vitez Brigade. We have a signature here that appears at the bottom of the document. Do you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: It's the signature of, as far as I'm aware, of Mr. Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have now reviewed several of the files that appear in the second binder, the lists that appear in the first binder. I can speak about every single soldier in the same manner, but that would take us too long, and I don't think it will be useful and necessary. But I hope that you have understood the approach and methodology that was used in this analysis by the Office of the Prosecutor and its investigators. Of course, I tender this into evidence, that is, the documents contained in the two binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The second binder, according to mine, is numbered Exhibit 2813.2. Is that right? I have it on the back of the binder. I don't know who put it on. It may have been the legal officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document -- oh, yes. It's the reference of the table that has been given to you. The binder itself has not been marked, and it contains separate exhibits. The only reference that we have is here, but each exhibit has its own mark, its own number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be sensible too, for future reference, to have the binder, as a whole, marked, and since we are not going to admit the schedule, perhaps it could have the same number. It would save me having to change this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 2813.2 can be the binder. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. Before cross-examination, I don't know if you've been told, for purposes of timetabling, if possible, I would be grateful for a short hearing at the end of the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been told. We will take a break at about half past three, continue for a period afterwards, depending on how we get on, and then, of course, at the end or after the break, we will have your hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just suggest, since you raised a number issue, we are indeed having two binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The first binder contains exhibits all of which have got numbers. It's the second one which contains additional material, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. I just ask in order to make not too many words when putting the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Spork. I have certain documents here, and I would like to ask you some questions. I think it's virtually impossible to discuss every single document, and by using our right to cross-examine witnesses, I will restrict myself to certain -- to a limited number of issues. And in our case, we will be addressing each issue separately. As regards the first binder containing general documents, we have a document that was issued by the command of the Vitez Brigade on the 24th of April, 1993. The number is the number of the brigade, and we have another number here which is your number, Z808. The document is a typed one. It was signed by Mr. Zvonimir Cilic, and we agreed with what you said about Mr. Zvonimir Cilic, and we agree with what is written here, a member of the command of the Vitez Brigade in charge of information. Could you please tell me if you have ever seen the original of this document bearing the signature of Mr. Cilic?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I have not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us anything about the origin of this document and how it ended up with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware of, sir, this document was seized during the search in Vitez in September 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you not aware of the fact that the Defence tendered this document in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm sorry for that, sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] It's okay, it's okay. It's too many documents, I agree. [Interpretation] At the beginning of your testimony, you mentioned a search that you carried out while you were explaining to us your methods, and you mentioned names that did not appear anywhere else. So the number of names decreased as you progressed through your investigation, because you could link certain names with specific events and facts, but there were also names which could not be linked to any specific events. Am I correct in understanding your method?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: If I may say so, the names that were mentioned by the different witnesses were not giving -- or the statements were not giving that many particulars, so we were not able to follow up on that name, because as we are all aware of in Bosnia, many people have the same surname and first name and occasionally also father's name, which made it very difficult to be sure that the name mentioned by the witness was the same one as mentioned on the listing. So we needed more particulars on the alleged member to be sure that we were -- that the witness was talking about the same person that was mentioned in one of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the course of your work -- or let me rephrase it. Do you have any previous knowledge about Bosnia, about their customs, names, religion, and so on and so forth? I mean before you started working here.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do. Actually, I was involved in several investigations with the Dutch police force involved -- where former inhabitants of the former Yugoslavia were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excellent. So the territory was not completely new to you, you had some previous knowledge. Thanks to that knowledge and thanks to the results of investigations, you will agree with me that we can conclude that very often we have the same names appearing on the same area. I'm referring now to surnames.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you also -- were you able to establish that certain names of villages or towns were the same as the surname of the family who lived there?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me give you an example. Haskici, were you able to conclude anything as to the origin of that name?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Not of that name, sir. But, for instance, I could give you an example like Santici and Santic, it's similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. So we can agree on that. Sometimes the name of the village is linked to the family name, but sometimes it is not, or maybe it can only be a part of the village that is linked with a certain family name. However, we have very often predominant family names in a certain area. Let us take the example of the Haskic family. Could you, perhaps, link that to Donja Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think that you personally -- or maybe your colleagues did interviews with at least 10 or 12 people by the family name of Haskic, and they were all from Donja Veceriska. Were you not able to establish that?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: As I explained this morning, sir, the statements, as they were, were of 98 different witnesses. Some of these witnesses gave two or three statements which were reviewed by the team, because it is impossible to do it all yourself. At least I can tell for myself, I've never interviewed somebody from Donja Veceriska with the name of Haskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Having mentioned Donja Veceriska, let us take the family name of Drmic, it's a Croatian family name. Were you able to observe that there were several people by the family name of Drmic and that they were all, or almost all of them, from Donja Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: The name of Drmic was identified in the witness statements. If they were all from the village of Donja Veceriska, I don't dare to say no. I should have to consult the documents in relation to each of these individual persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Several people by the surname of Drmic were identified, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me sum up this subject. I think it is indisputable that from the village of Ahmici, at least two-thirds of the witnesses who testified here were people by the name of Ahmic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we can conclude that the family name itself is sometimes not enough in order to identify certain villages. Now, let us talk about the Christian names. In Croatian, we have names such as Ante, Dragan, and so on, and such Christian names are very common in that area. There is a limited number of preferred names in a certain area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Therefore, in order for us to be able to identify a certain person, we have to have other identifying information as well. We have to know the place of residence, preferably the name of the father. That doesn't mean a lot, because, again, it can be the same as some other name. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I would agree when we say that in the area we are talking about now, more than one person could have the same first name, surname, and father's name. Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, so as to be absolutely sure in terms of identification of a certain individual, we have to go further on and have the place and date of birth. You also mentioned a citizen's number when speaking about individual people. When you did so, I had the impression that you were referring to the military identification number. This is the number that we can see, for example, on the list of the Novi Travnik Battalion. I don't remember the number. I believe it was Z505, in section 12 of the general documents binder.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What does this number mean to you? How do you interpret it?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: The first two figures are the date of birth; the second --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Actually, it is not necessary to know the exact interpretation. But just tell me whether this was a military identification number or a number given to every civilian in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I can't tell you that, sir. The only thing I know is that many people who were soldiers in, let's say, the HVO had a military identification number, which consisted of date and year of birth, plus a specific number in relation to this person, and that, in total, made it the military identification number, as they were mentioned in the big 92nd Home Guard Regiment list. Because on that list, we also found many people without a military identification number, which means that -- I assume, and that's an assumption -- if everybody would have a specific number in the former Yugoslavia, it should have been mentioned on this list, or it would have been mentioned on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: These are two speculate issues. Let us try to distinguish between them. So you don't know that every citizen in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, every citizen had this so-called -- if I'm not mistaken, it used to be called the citizen's personal number. Later on, the term changed somewhat. So you didn't know that. You didn't know that every citizen of the former Yugoslavia had to have a number like that.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I'm aware of the fact that every citizen in the former Yugoslavia had a number, because I know that in a previous investigation, when we investigated the casualties of Ahmici, when we tried to obtain the death certificates, we went first to the birth certificate, which gives a number and a date of birth, which would then be passed on to when the involved person was married, so the marriage certificate, and eventually when that person would pass away, that number would proceed to the death -- I can't recollect the exact name of it, but there was some kind of a document which was made in each municipality showing that on such and such date, a person with this and this identification number had died or was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. So I believe we can agree that since every soldier, who was at the same time a citizen, had to have that number.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm not sure if the number would have to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you think that there are military numbers, military identification numbers as well, and that, for example, Goran Babic, the first name that appears on the list, that the number indicated next to his name was his military identification number, but that he also had a citizen's personal number. Or does it mean that if Goran Babic died, if I look him up under the military identification number, I will not be able to find him; however, if the number is the so-called citizen's personal number, then I will be able to find him.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Which document are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was just an example. I took it from section number 12. It's from the Novi Travnik HVO. It was on the first page of the document, the name under number 1, Goran Babic, or Babic, Franjo Goran. But you can take any name like that; the situation is always the same.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: It could be that in the situation of the former Yugoslavia, that this personal identification number which was given to a person as soon as he was born, that that same number would be used as his military identification number. Nevertheless, it still shows the date and year of birth, plus a specific number in relation -- because the total, the date and year of birth, plus the specific number, identifies the person as being that specific person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That is the structure of the number. The number contains the date of birth -- day, month, year -- which is followed by the code for relevant register; we also have a figure for the sex and the relevant municipality. So this is all for the purposes of local administration, and we can agree on that. Mr. Spork, you said that you spent a number of years working for the Dutch police and that you also had some relevant experience concerning the former Yugoslavia. In the late '70s, early '80s, there were quite a few illegal Gypsies from the former Yugoslavia in the Netherlands which were deported back to the former Yugoslavia because their status here was illegal. However, the problem of identification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I'm going to stop you. The question is two paragraphs long already. Could you shorten the questions? But, in fact, we're going to adjourn now for a quarter of an hour. Can you finish this witness conveniently this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sure. Your Honour, I really don't have the intention of going document by document. I will only open issues which obviously should be discussed later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now for a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us then finish with this subject. Perhaps just for the sake of illustration, as a member of the Royal Dutch Police, were you ever involved in any matters dealing with the deportation of former Yugoslav citizens, I mean the Romany, in particular, back to Yugoslavia sometime in the early '80s, perhaps, and late '70s? It was quite a problem in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, sir, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. So let us then go back and round off the first subject. So this long list, 353, that we spoke about, V.P. 1779, that is what it says, and if we turn a couple of pages just at random, we see that for quite a number of persons, the number of the military booklet is missing. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is practically a rule that a soldier has a document of one kind or another, and we saw it already, because that is one of the identification documents, documents by which military can be identified. We agree about that?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Also, quite a number of people, perhaps a little less than in the former case but quite a number of persons, some 15 or maybe even 20 percent of persons on the list, also do not have the personal number of the citizens, and we mentioned that was also another important identification element; is that true?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: As I said before, sir, I'm not sure if it is a citizen number or military identification number. The only thing I'm aware of, I think it's not 15 or 20 percent, it's less, because as far as I remember, most of the names contain at least the date, month, and year of birth, but they don't include the last six numbers. But that isn't 15 to 20 percent. I would say much less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Less, but some are missing. I can really do the calculations sometime tomorrow. But some of them do not have here -- some of those who are listed here do not have their personal numbers in this list?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Some of them do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Quite. Incidentally, I did not see the translation of this document, but I should like to warn you, as regards this number in the first column after the name, it says here "JMBG", and that was the former acronym for that personal number that this talks about. But since we all have this list before us, let us look at it, the first page.
