During the examination-in-chief, my client, Mario Cerkez, was mentioned, and he appears on page 1 of this list, and then it would be twice, and there is a signature then, and all the other individuals also have their signatures affixed here. So I conclude it's true, I do have an advantage over you because I know how this list was compounded, but evidently each one of these witnesses had to put his signature on this list. In other words, the list was compounded on the basis of somebody's report, presumably the person himself or somebody else, and a signature was a confirmation that this information is true. That is, every person listed here confirms, with his signature, that the information here is authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I mentioned before, just before the adjournment, you're not giving evidence. Can you kindly confine yourself to asking simple questions rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, sir. I was trying to shorten the thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So we are agreed that there is a signature accompanying every name?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: We are, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And let us still look at Mario Cerkez here. Are you claiming that this is his signature?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: According to the list, it should be, but I'm not qualified to say if it is his signature because I wasn't present when the signature was written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Very correct. Thank you, sir. [Interpretation] Let us take one example more. On the page with ordinal numbers beginning 1227, it's halfway through and is somewhere midway through the list, so in the middle of the page -- have you managed to find it? And then it goes on, that is, the names then go down to number 1237, so ten persons. The first two are Dragan Bobas and Ljuban Bobas, and the last one is -- I think it says Marina Bobas, and perhaps one after her, Grebenar -- yes, Marina Bobas, Marina Bobas is the last one, yes. And now look at this column on the right where the signatures are. One does not need an expert in graphology to see that they had all been signed the same way, that is, initials in the same hand and in the same way, and it is quite legible, I should say, that it was signed by a person called N. Bobas?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: It looks like it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] It looks like it. So much about this list. Of course, there are many other things, but I will not raise them for the moment. Let me ask you about a couple of documents from the smaller binder where we have documents, not the person files. [Interpretation] Let us go back to the list under 2, where we saw Cilic's signature, but typed, and the list of killed Vitezovi, that is, members of that Vitez unit. As a matter of fact, it was produced with the last witness, with the previous witness. The first part of this list refers to the killed, and the names under 2, a person named Lovro Kolak, and then 20, Zoran Ramljak, and 3, Ivo Zuljevic, they also figure in the list of killed Vitezovi, that is, members of the Vitezovi unit.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Are you referring to this list, sir? I mean, the list we are looking at, Exhibit Z808, it says, obviously, "List of Vitezovi Brigade soldiers killed in the conflict." I'm not aware if they were also mentioned on another list, if this list is not included in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Very well. I wanted to ask you if you remember seeing the list of the killed members of the Vitez Brigade -- no, excuse me -- list of killed members of the Vitezovi unit, because we have not been handed over that list.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Because I didn't review that list, sir, because my single -- the single purpose of this exercise was to identify members of the Viteska Brigade and not members of the Vitezovi, which does not exclude that it could be that members of the Vitezovi have also been members of the Viteska Brigade, because they could have been lent, one to the other. But, as I said before, I was just concentrating on names, dates of birth, and specific items that could identify a member of the Viteska Brigade, and this document which was tendered, as you said before, gives us names of people that were also mentioned on our list of identified members of the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned this, just a short side question. As you investigated those people on the various lists, did you happen to notice that some people spent some time in one unit and then moved on to another unit?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Not via this investigation, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on to the next document, that is, the same binder, same binder, but the one under 3. When one looks at it, one should say that this was from a computer. These were lists which were done on a computer, if one looks at the original, the Alfa Force, the list of 35 names. It looks like a computer list. Have you ever seen the original of this document, or do you have it, perhaps, in your files?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, I don't have it, sir. This is the document I obtained via our database, which means that it could be that the original is in the evidence folder, but at least this is a copy of the document that's in our possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know, how did this document reach the Prosecutor's office? What is the source of this document?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, I don't, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The title says that it was issued by the command OS -- we're not quite sure if we know what that acronym means -- of Central Bosnia; is that correct? That is what one reads at the top.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes. At the top, it says: "The Alfa Force Reconnaissance Sabotage Group was formed on the 6th of April, 1992, on an order of the Central Bosnia OS Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: True. And then one of the members, and let's move on to the next document, that is, the document under 4, that these members received their salaries, are paid. And then it says, "Central Bosnia, the command of the Operative Zone," so you would know that institution, and it is signed by the commander of the Operative Zone. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this Alfa Force evidently has nothing to do with the brigade. You know what was the Operative Zone and the commander of the Operative Zone, that he was a superior to the accused Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Generally, what the document says is that it is signed by Colonel Tihomir Blaskic. I haven't found anything that would assure me or my colleagues that that also means that this Alfa Force has never been under the command of Mr. Mario Cerkez. It just means that as commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, it is obvious that Mr. Blaskic -- Colonel Blaskic, in this situation, signed for paying the amount of money to these several unit members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. Very well. But tell me, please, apart from those six names which are circled and you believe that are in some other lists that you managed to identify, that is, that they appear in some documents which are associated with the Vitez Brigade, but other persons here are also associated with the Vitez Brigade, the rest of the 29 of them.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: [Answer obscured by translation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On this list, six names are circled, and then these persons appear in individual files. So when you subtract them from 35, it's 29. You do not identify those 29 as members of the brigade, at least we did not find it. Is it that, in your opinion, they were not that?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: The people that are circled on this list are the people of which we have personal files, and the only thing this document says is that obviously he was paid as a member of the Alfa Force Sabotage Group. As I said before, according to our investigation, this doesn't mean necessarily that -- being a member of a special unit, that doesn't mean that this unit can't be under the control, or under the direct supervision or command of Mr. Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. So you are not identifying them by people but by the structure, by the organisation. Now, let me ask you, have you seen a document -- do you think there is a document which would show that Alfa Force would be a unit -- part of the Vitez Brigade? Have you ever seen such a document?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, I have not, sir. But, as I said before, the reason for this identification of possible members of the Viteska Brigade meant that when we went through the databases, we brought in the names of the people that were recognised and of which we could reasonably think that they were members of the Viteska Brigade, and once we did that, names came up and documents came up, and one of these documents is this one. So my assumption in this would then be that if he was a member of the Viteska Brigade, and he was also a member of the Alfa Force, that this unit was under the command of the commander of the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you for repeating the explanation, but will you please answer the question, and it is very simple. Have you ever seen in your work at the Prosecutor's office, ever, a document, any kind of document -- a military order or an organisational chart or any document at all -- from which one could conclude that a unit called Alfa Force was subordinated to the Vitez Brigade, that is, that it was a component, an element, of the Vitez Brigade? Yes or no, please. We've already heard the explanation.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Not as far as I can recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct. Never. This document does not have a signature or a stamp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It doesn't have a date either.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: The date says, "3rd of November, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I cannot find it, I don't see any date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Z265, under the tab number 4, has the date the 3rd of November. But you're right, the other one doesn't have a date. We can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is Z67, that one doesn't have a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In respect to that, have you noticed from the documents issued in Bosnia that we, unlike here in Europe, attach a lot of importance to stamps. Every document, every serious document must have a stamp. Have you noticed that custom?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I have to admit that I've seen a lot of documents with stamps, but I've also seen documents without stamps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As an illustration, this long list has even two stamps. Some people think that it might add to the reliability of the document. However, the document number 67 does not have a stamp. Z265, in section 4, signed by Blaskic, also has a stamp. Let us have a look at number 5. It is the document Z1299.2, in section 5 of the binder. Have you seen the original of this document?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that, again, we have a computer printout?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree that it doesn't have a signature or a stamp?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The title of the document says it is a list of the wounded members of the brigade. What does the date on the left-hand side mean, that is, the 12th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I assume that this was the date that this document was produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about the source of the document and how it reached the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I cannot because, as I said before, during this search in September 1998, we seized an enormous amount of documents, and these documents were put into the database by this office. The purpose of this investigation was not to authenticate the documents that were in our possession but to find the names of people that were mentioned by the witnesses. So I cannot tell you exactly where this document comes from, but according to my knowledge, about 90 percent of the documents that have been put into these binders, they were directly related to the search of 1998. But, no, sir, I cannot specifically say if this was one of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on that occasion -- I'm not referring to every location, but only the two that are of interest for us -- that they were seized at a municipal building?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I can't tell you that because I was not involved in these two locations. I was on the third location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since you don't know that, can you exclude the possibility that that document was composed in the Defence Office, that is, in the civilian section of the municipal government?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it is a bit difficult to speak about the value of names if we are not sure about the authenticity of the document, in view of what you have just said, that your objective was not to ascertain the authenticity of the document but to link the names with the names mentioned by witnesses?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I don't necessarily agree, because during a criminal investigation, once one does a search, the documents -- in this situation, the documents that you obtain are supposed to be authentic; I mean, at least they have been made in that office or at least they were kept in that office, and should, as such, be a document in relation to that organisation, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the location where you were, was the computer's hard disk taken as well?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, we did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that this document is actually the printout from that hard disk? If you don't remember that, it's not important. I should take this opportunity -- I do not have pages 14 and 15 that is completely legible. The last page that is legible is page number 13. I want to check whether you have pages 14 and 15, from numbers 651 to 661, and there's also something written on the last page. But I just cannot read it. Do you have the two pages in question? The number of the last illegible page is 0080838. I don't know whether that document contains a signature, or a stamp, or some other markings. Are those two pages legible in your binder?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I have these two pages, and they are illegible on my binder too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the penultimate page contains the list from 651 to 661, but there is a certain text on the last page, and I would like to know whether that page, the last one, contains any identifying information such as signature or a stamp.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, sir, because my page is the same as yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The next list is the list of the killed members. I'm referring to section 6, document Z996.3. Looking at the document, I think it's more or less the same type of document. It says: "List of Killed Members of the HVO and Civilians." Again, in the header of the document, we see the Vitez Brigade. Do you think it's logical for a brigade to have also lists of killed civilians? Did you find any other document that would explain such an unusual procedure?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a comment, it's a comment. Yes, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The source of this document is the same as for previous documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: It should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we don't have to discuss the issue of signature and stamp again. Next is a document 750.1 in section 7 of the binder. Is the source of that document the same again?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I assume so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us have a look at the signature. There is something added in handwriting at the end of the document on the second page, some kind of note, and then at the very end of the document we have "Commander Mario Cerkez". This was probably prepared by an official and the document had to be signed by someone. In this case, it was signed -- it was supposed to be signed by Mario Cerkez. Does your copy contain the handwritten signature as well?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As I can see under the name of Mario Cerkez, there are three other places, three numbers. I don't see any names on my copy.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Neither on mine, sir, and you have the same copy as I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One last thing about this document. The handwritten part, there is a sentence here in handwriting which precedes the name. [In English] [Previous interpretation continues] ... "soldiers were members of the Vitez Brigade who were killed." [Interpretation] This does not correspond to the Croatian text, because the Croatian text contains the word "casualties", which can include wounding and killing. This is not specific enough, so I should ask this translation to be corrected again. Some of them may have actually survived, but some may have been killed as well. The next document is the document Z1337.1 in section 8 of the binder, and I assume that it was obtained in the same manner.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Umm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As regards this document, we have several categories, several categories of persons which were apparently killed. Apparently this is a list of killed persons. The first names refer to the situation before the 16th of April, 1993. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: However, the remaining information concerns the relevant sector, obligatory work, member of the brigade command, so these are different categories of persons listed here?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: When I look at this document, sir, I would say that this document which was drafted, according to the date, on the 20th of December, 1993, that the people that were killed before the 16th of April, 1992, were put together, and then it was specified after -- as of the 16th of April, 1993, where the specific person belonged to or what part of the working area he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It's a logical conclusion, because we have the category. It is stated here, and that was my line of thinking as well. But except for the first ten persons who refer to the situation before the 16th of April, 1993, this is no longer the case. That's why I stated the subheadings. Let us take the next category, for example, the brigade command. We have one person only, Borislav Josic, and here the date is the date of the death of the individual in question, the 31st of August, 1993. So all of the remaining categories contain dates of death, but those dates are the ones after the 16th of April, 1993, or at least starting with that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the title or the heading, as you explained it to us, that is, the situation before the 16th of April, 1993, concerns only the ten persons listed in the first section?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: The way I read this document, sir, is that this document gives an overview of men that were killed, the first ten in relation to the period before the 16th of April, and after -- the others, between the 16th of April and the 20th of December, 1993, when this document was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. So only the first ten individuals concern the situation before the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been over this, Mr. Kovacic. Please, let's go on. We can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us not waste any more time on that. Just confirm that the source of the document is the same as for the previous three or four documents.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps one additional question. Have you ever seen, in your analysis, a document enabling you to conclude that the members of the detail units would be actually members of the Vitez Brigade itself?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards the next document, section 9, document Z957.1, I should just ask you to comment on the note of page 5 of the Croatian original. I believe that it should be page 6 of the translation. Did you take this remark into account when you followed further on the names that were contained in the list?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you did take into account the contents of this remark. The remark actually speaks about certain oversights, as far as I can see. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Not necessarily. The remark says that during the course of the fighting, a lot of people who were not members of the units before joined the fighting on their side, so the list might not be complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Again, this document was signed by Mr. Cilic. This particular document contains the signature itself?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The document under number 10, Z1372.1, I'm interested in the title of the document, which states as follows: "List of Soldiers Killed in the Zone of Responsibility of the 5th Battalion". Looking at this list containing 16 persons, can you conclude that all these persons were members of this battalion, which was part of the Vitez Brigade? Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, I cannot, because the document obviously says, "Killed in the Zone of Responsibility," which does not necessarily mean that they were members of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the names that have been encircled, the five names that are dealt with later on, could have been killed in the zone of responsibility of the battalion and thereby enter the list of the wounded or the killed, and on the basis of that, we conclude that they were actually members of that unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, sir, because the people that were encircled are persons of whom we found other documents in relation which would show that they were members of the Vitez Brigade. That's why these five were selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well then. Did you ever -- sorry, let me rephrase my question. Section 11, document Z1324.1, the document that was signed by a certain Mrs. Mira Vrebac, did you manage to identify that person on the basis of some other documents? Did you maybe see her name in any other document?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: You're talking about Mrs. Vrebac? No. But as I said before, I was not looking for this name, because this name was not mentioned by the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: However, she is the author of the document, but never mind. Attached to this document are two empty documents with an official heading. It seems that someone had access to official documents of a certain institution which were actually not used while composing this document. Are you sure that these documents were found together, and could you perhaps explain to us why these empty documents are attached to the document which was compiled by Mrs. Vrebac? Is there any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: The reason for this is so that, as I can see it now, but I'm looking at the area numbers, this means that both documents were obtained together, so as a package, and therefore they were brought into the system as a package, because the U.N. numbers are following up corresponding U.N. numbers which, as I said before, means that they must have been seized as a package.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You have obviously reviewed a large number of documents that were seized there, but have you noticed that this type of document was used -- does this type of document with the header like this has been used elsewhere, that the same heading was used, and then the Defence office would also mention its title? It was also used by the Defence office? Have you noticed that?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, I have not, sir, but as I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have come to the list Z505 in section 12, which was composed on the 27th of February, 1993. Again, it's a computer printout. According to this printout, if we sum up every entry, we realise that the number of persons mentioned here is 433. I may have made a mistake, but I think this is approximately the number. Have you counted them?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Unlike other documents, this list is very precise in the sense that it gives citizens personal numbers for every person, as well as the address and other necessary identifying information. The relevant identifying information, that is, the citizen's personal number, address, date of birth, has been indicated in, if not in all cases, then at least in 99 percent of them. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: It gives the PIN address, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: PIN address, P-I-N address.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Oh, that is what you call it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, could you please explain to us, because are you speaking about this list in detail, we would like to know if you are disputing this list, the list of persons here. This is the question. We are not investigating for the sake of investigating here. The question is whether there is a list and if this list is disputed by you or not. We are talking about it in detail, and personally I don't quite understand how we are progressing in our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm disputing every single document here except for this one. However, I have to check certain details. But as far as I can see, it's an authentic document, and except for two or three other documents that have also been admitted here, that is as far as the authenticity of the document is concerned. As regards all other documents, I dispute all of them. This is only what these documents purport to be. I mean we cannot be sure. I can give you one more example, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- our argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us move on. At some stage, you can tell us why you dispute the authenticity of these documents. Now, they appear to speak for themselves, but let us move on now. Do you need to ask any more questions about any more?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do agree with you, that we should not waste any more time on these documents. I am challenging their authenticity, and I will call my evidence to prove it. However, I should use two or three more examples from this file which can show us the unreliability of such material. As regards this particular binder, Witness, would you please have a look at section 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to go through these documents. We've been over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to show you a name so that we can search for it in the folder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In that document, Z957.1, under number 45, I'm using this only as an illustration, Adis Cosic's name is mentioned, father's name Ejub. That particular person can be found in the large list, mentioned again -- I apologise, I don't have it here -- we have him in the list of the military police, the list which was given to us together with the documents of the previous witness, under the number 37. I would like the witness to explain the fact that we have one and the same person listed under two units, and let us take this only as an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Spork, can you say anything more than what appears in the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I couldn't, sir. I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I could go on with a number of examples and illustrations, and that would require some additional documents, but this is obviously not the right time. We will be calling our own evidence as to that. However, I still have a few general questions maybe. No, I believe I have finished with the general issues as well. If you will just allow me to add, before I conclude. While we were discussing the testimony of this witness, my learned colleague, Mr. Nice, mentioned our defence, mentioned our argument. I will just say, and we will prove it later on, that the Vitez Brigade was never actually in Ahmici. I wanted the record to reflect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a totally different point. Are you disputing, Mr. Kovacic, are you disputing that the 38 individuals mentioned in the second binder were members of the Vitez Brigade or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Except one or two, at present, I cannot say that. What I mean is some of them were members of the Vitez Brigade at some point in time, which means, in view of the time when the Vitez Brigade was founded, it could have been sometime in summer or sometime, perhaps, in autumn, perhaps after the period for which Mr. Cerkez is indicted. What I do dispute is that any one of those 38 was a member of the Vitez Brigade on the 16th of April, or that he committed a crime as a member of the Vitez Brigade. There are some individuals who joined the brigade in August or September, for instance; there are some people who never were members of the brigade; there may be some who were with the brigade in May, then they went to another unit, and then they came back in June. But I dispute that those people were members of the Vitez Brigade, as it is put to us here, and that they committed crimes as members of that brigade. There are also some persons who were so-called -- and I'm referring to 1992 -- who were so-called shift soldiers, that is, a soldier would be called up to go to the front line with the Serbs, and he would go there, he would be treated as a military, and then he would go back to his place, he would go back to work in his factory, or work his land, or whatever. And if he committed the crime at that particular time, then he is not a member of the unit at that particular time. That is our view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if I may, just a very brief comment to begin with. I listened to Mr. Kovacic. The Vitez Brigade is evidently a brigade one joins and then leaves whenever one wants. They are part-time soldiers when they have time because they are not working the land, or whatever. All I wanted to ask the witness, Mr. Spork, is if he could simply tell us something about the soldier called Zoran Matosevic, a soldier figuring under 39, entry 39. Does he know something about his lot?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is true, Mr. Spork, that this soldier was killed on the 11th of June, 1993, that is, on the day when the convoy known as the Convoy of Joy was blocked in the area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who killed that soldier?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: He was killed by members of BritBat, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I should like to show you a document, a copy of a document, naturally, which seems to show -- where we see that he was killed, and this is the document 2807/2. I should also like to show you, once again, a document that we discussed this morning and which has to do with the soldier Zoran Sero.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As for the Zoran Matosevic document, there is a signature and there is a name.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. Mr. Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is also the name -- or, rather, this signature is identical with the one which we found on the identity card issued to Zoran Sero.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I'm not an expert, but I would say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, are those documents from the files? It seems not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on. Let's come to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic showed to you the big list, and here Mario Cerkez appears as the first member of the 92nd Brigade. We were shown the signature of Mr. Cerkez, and, yes, indeed, we see that Mr. Cerkez's signature varies, we have different signatures. And this is the list of the 92nd Regiment, these are the same, but it is, again, the same signature here I've shown you, not the one that we see here in the long list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am about to finish, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's not a handwriting expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Carry Spork, again, a clarification as regards the list, the list 808, that is, the list signed by Mr. Cilic. In the transcript it says that, but I believe it was your slip of the tongue, that it is a list of the members of the Vitezovi killed in Vitez, but it is a list of members of the Vitez Brigade, or Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, that was a slip of the tongue. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about the Alfa Force, about that unit, and there is a list where there are a number of names, the first known name on it is Kriss Wilson, and it is the document issued on the 3rd of November, 1992. Do you remember the document?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us that this same Kriss Wilson, when he was wounded in Novi Travnik, on the 14th of October, 1992, that is, a few days earlier, that he said that his direct superior was Mario Cerkez, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: According to the certificate we have, yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You verified two of those soldiers, Bralo and Perica Vukadinovic, and after the verification that you undertook, were those two soldiers ever condemned for the offences they committed in Bosnia in 1992 and 1993 -- 1994. Excuse me. 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You undertook the verification of two of those soldiers, soldier Miroslav Bralo and another one called Perica Vukadinovic, with the Bosnian authorities. And the information that was communicated to you, did it show that those two soldiers were condemned for the crimes committed in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Maybe I totally misunderstood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about the interpretation. I was trying to be quite clear in what I said. I'm asking you if, to your knowledge, the two soldiers, Miroslav Bralo and Perica Vukadinovic, were penally charged in Bosnia for the crimes they committed in 1992 and 1993, whether they were brought to trial for those?

utterances.speaker: CARRY SPORK
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Spork, thank you for coming to give your evidence. That concludes it. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not a matter that Mr. Spork could have dealt with, I think, and therefore there was no point in interrupting the flow of cross-examination, but I would have thought that if any of the apparent signatures of the defendant Cerkez were to be challenged, if it's not made plain in our case, then, of course, the matter can be dealt with in rebuttal. Alternatively, if it is made plain, it might conceivably, although we are pressed for time, be dealt with in our case. But, in any event, it simply hasn't been made plain, so we can't deal with it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Likewise, the point raised by the Chamber, the authenticity or otherwise of documents has been dealt with in very global terms, and it would be impossible for us to do more effectively than to say that which Mr. Spork said about the general origin of documents seized in Vitez. And, again, absent further particularised notice from the Defence, we'll await to deal with those matters if and when clear evidence emerges to the effect that they are other than what they appear to be, speaking for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. There has been, I'm afraid, another witness waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but I suspect it's too late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's too late, it really is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He's from the building, he's been very understanding, and I'll take him first thing in the morning, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: With the apologies of the Court that he's been kept hanging about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I deal with one very short public matter in open court session. I'm happy to say that the diary of Mr. Ashdown is now available. It's been resupplied by him. Copies for the Defence, copies for the Chamber. It has the map, which, if you haven't seen it before, is quite interesting. We all know about the map that was written on the invitation card. It's attached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this the map that was produced at the dinner, the famous dinner?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the banquet and everything else. Copies for the Defence, as requested; copies for the Chamber. I can, in due course, slot it in as part of the statement -- of the transcript of the witness, but I thought that possibly as a little bit of interesting relief, it might come this afternoon. The map is on the last sheet. And it is a fairly steady hand, whatever the state of the dinner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't give the menu.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, but I think a good time was had by all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's one matter we want to deal with, apart from that, and that concerns the application for a video conference, which you have submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Some for next week --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- which is fairly short notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's right that the Defence should make any representations that they want about that, the application to have witnesses by video conference link next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We have not had a great deal of time to digest this, Mr. President, but in principle, I think the witnesses who are obviously sick or physically incapable of coming to The Hague represent a clearly exceptional circumstance, or it would certainly be in the interests of justice to minimise the inconvenience to them. We couldn't, and we don't object to those. That certainly covers most of the first witness in paragraph 2(a) of the application. With respect to the witness in paragraph 2(b), the last thing that we want to do is require this witness to travel to a foreign country while his wife is ill, and we have no particular objection to that application either. With respect to Witness 2(c), we frankly see no reason why he shouldn't be here. He doesn't appear to be sick. He appears to be subject to a subpoena, and it seems to me that if he's going to testify in the case, then he should do so here. With respect to Witness 2(d), let me defer to my colleagues representing the co-defendant on that. With respect to Witness 2(e), Your Honour, I am at a loss to understand why this witness needs to testify live. Surely this village witness falls into the category of those witnesses who have been victims. They've already testified at length in the Blaskic case. Presumably he or she has been fully questioned on all matters pertinent to this case. I simply do not understand why it's necessary for her to testify yet again and be subject to the pressures that perhaps don't need to be imposed upon her in that regard. And then with respect to Witness 3(a), here is a gentleman who has apparently undergone a recent operation and is not able to come to The Hague, and so that clearly seems to us to fall into the category of circumstances in which a videolink would be appropriate. I think that's our position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Too many papers, Your Honour. I will join whatever my colleagues have said, and the only thing which he left for us is the witness under item 2(d). I think that his name was restricted so far, so I will stick to the number. We think that there is some misunderstanding with that witness. It was promised many times that he would come and then that he would not come. Anyway, I would like to have this witness on direct/cross, if possible, here. But if that is not possible for any justifiable reasons, which I cannot find in this paragraph, then so be it. However, I do think that this witness should be brought here, if need there be, and of course that I also think that all other evidence we already tendered related to that incident are quite sufficient to understand the real probative value of statement of -- of testimony of that witness. That's about what we have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately I haven't got my own copy of the application with me, so I can't respond immediately, if any response is required, in relation to the names, but -- ah, we have found it at last. There's one thing I'll have to add about number 2(d), but I'll have to add that at the ex parte hearing. As to the one in respect of which Mr. Sayers raised objection, I think he's the one in respect of whom there's the wife problem, and it seems to me a perfectly reasonable attitude to adopt. His attitude is as it is, and time is short. If the videolink is going to be set up, there's absolutely no reason for him not to be taken in that way, and we would certainly ask you to look favourably on that application. I can tell you that in relation to one of the applicants, and if I can find it, it's not "E" -- no, "F", I think -- no, number "E", I think we're in the rather odd positions here that in the belt-and-braces exercise, that witness has provided an affidavit, and having provided an affidavit and at the time of providing an affidavit was asked what her attitude would be to giving evidence, the reply was, "I'll give evidence and come here to do so." So it may be that that witness would prefer now to come. The possibility of a videolink was offered, and I think the response was, "Well, you can either have the affidavit or you can have the evidence in The Hague," but there it is. So it may be that that witness will want to come to The Hague rather than to do it by videolink, which would seem to me to be much to the -- well, much preferable from the witness's point of view, but there it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you continuing the application or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think probably, at the moment, not, because I think -- I'll have to deal with the question of affidavit tomorrow. Maybe the witness can give the evidence by affidavit and that will be that. But the other three -- and there's something I've got to say about the one in ex parte hearing, and so that would leave only the three, in reality, because I don't think there's any prospect of that other one being a witness by video in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I was going to ask the legal officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, are there any other matters before we go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was a miscommunication, Mr. President, but I thought that I had said that with respect to Witness 2(B) in the application, the gentleman whose wife is in the hospital in Travnik, we did not oppose that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps for the better planning of the Prosecution, we should say what you ask us to state on the open transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with that tomorrow, as it's getting late.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Indeed, if I may, Your Honour, just to mention one thing also just for better planning. It is not that we will raise issue on the authenticity of the Cerkez signature, yes, with us, for this is a particular document. But mainly all the -- and we will bring in the case a lot of -- some are already in the case. We will tender many orders signed by Cerkez personally, so there is no chance that we would raise that issue. But this one, yes. And talking about documents, my learned colleague mentioned something like that we have to prove that those documents are not correct. We should also consider that in a broader picture as who is having the burden of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. These are all points you can make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, unless there's anything else before we go into ex parte session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think so, save to give notice, the tape tomorrow, possibly a witness dealing with provenance of the bulk of the remaining documents in general, village binders, and discuss about the videos. That's what I was planning for tomorrow's menu.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to the taped witness, we don't know who it is and we don't know what they are going to say. And with respect to the identification of documents witness, once again we don't know who that witness is or what they are going to say. I wonder if we might just request some information along those lines so that we can prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. No doubt that could be provided in some short form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll deal with it by telephone or otherwise overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll tell my friends afterwards about the taped witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll rise for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 5.11 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 25th day of February, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
